speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (for the Minister of Public Works) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the Minister of Public Works on behalf of His Majesty to enter into an agreement to pay to the corporation of the city of Ottawa the sum of $100,000 for the year ending July 1, 1942.
He said:	His Excellency the Governor
General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, February 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Alphonse Fournier for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, will you permit me first of all, on rising to take part in this debate, to tell you that I am particularly nervous, not only because of the strain which naturally comes from the necessity or thought of making a speech, but also because of the stress which surrounds everyone who takes part in this debate owing to the bitterness which has

The Address-Mr. Turgeon
been aroused, not so much in this house but in the country at large, in connection with the subject matter of any speech made to-day by an hon. member on the motion to present an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to the speech from the throne.
It is my intention to deal frankly and bluntly with some of the questions at issue and with some of the agitation which is being aroused outside of this house.
First of all, however, may I deal with a more pleasing thing. May I join with other members who have spoken by paying a tribute to the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier) and the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) for the excellent addresses with which they opened this debate. I feel that they did better because of the experiences they had among the people of the British isles. It is too bad that it is not possible for every hon. member to do what these hon. members were able to do-visit Great Britain during this time of stress. I did not have the honour of hearing the mover and the seconder, but I read their speeches, and one who heard them or one who read them can tell that both hon. members spoke not only from their own points of view but also from that emotion which was aroused in them because of what they saw among the people of Great Britain. They found men and women like ourselves protecting their lives and their homes, and looking after their children-who after all are like our own children. May I leave this thought with the house and with certain sections of the people of Canada, that these hon. members found in the British isles a people who were not fighting for the spreading or for the maintenance and perpetuation of imperialism, but against the most ruthless expansion of imperialism that the world has ever seen. Neither we nor the people of the British isles are fighting for imperialism. We are defending ourselves against it. And the courage which has been shown by the people of Great Britain is precisely that quality which Doctor Johnson said was the first condition of virtue, because without it there can be no virtue. They were fighting, as some day we may have to fight, for home, for fireside, and for children.
To turn now to another matter, I have noticed lately, in spite of this demand for conscription, of which I shall speak later, that county councils and other organizations are demanding of this government that it stop taking men from agricultural communities into the armed forces of Canada. That demand has been made not only in the province of Quebec-which I mention because
it is on the lips of nearly everyone outside this chamber who has taken part in the discussion of this question-but also in Ontario and other parts of English-speaking Canada. In my own riding of Cariboo there is a shortage of farm labour. Our cattle men do not know how they will make their hay next fall. Our grain growers and our farmers who are dealing with ordinary agriculture are in exactly the same position. I do not want anyone to misunderstand me. I feel that at a time such as we are now entering it is the duty of every member of parliament, not only to argue this matter and try to create public opinion, although that is a supreme task, but also to make his position clear so that the people whom we directly represent, and the people of all Canada whom also each one of us represents, shall have no doubt as to where we stand.
It is therefore my intention to state clearly at the outset, though probably I shall return to it later, that I have every intention of supporting the plebiscite proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I voted, when in uniform overseas, against conscription in 1917. I had not the faintest hesitation in voting against it, not because of conscription in itself, but because of the dastardly associations which surrounded it at that time. To-day I am not unmindful of the same associations that some people are trying to weave about it, but I am quite ready to trust this government, and, naturally, particularly the Prime Minister, in dealing with the various situations as they may arise. Again without hesitation, so that everybody will know where I stand, I say it is my intention, after this plebiscite is taken and the people vote favourably upon it, as I sincerely hope they will in every province of Canada, to support every measure of compulsory service-I am not afraid of the word "conscription"-that the Prime Minister and those who are surrounding him in government may think it necessary to bring to the people of Canada.
Wendell Willkie, speaking some time ago, said that democracy rises to its greatest heights at its worst moments. I am afraid that to-day we in Canada are entering upon one of the evil moments, if not the worst moment, of democracy. We talk of leadership.
I wonder if hon. members who speak of leadership every time they make a recommendation which is not accepted, realize that we are so formed that sometimes we recognize leadership only when leadership agrees with * our own opinions, and that we are inclined to say there is lack of leadership when a leader goes in a direction contrary to that in which we want him to go.
The Address-Mr. Turgeon

I intend to say something to-day about leadership, with particular reference to leadership at the present moment, having in mind among other things, naturally, this plebiscite and the leadership that is being given us so that from time to time we may be able to continue the total war effort which we have been making without arousing too many of those basic prejudices which of themselves, when brought to the surface, interfere with our full effort-leadership at the present moment, which after all merges so fast into the future. In speaking thus, one must not forget the immediate past, in spite of the fact that it has been streaming so swiftly by us that all of it to-day is obscured and most of it forgotten.
I remember something of the fateful session of September, 1939, which authorized this government to declare war on behalf of Canada against Germany. As I remember, we met on Thursday; we started the address on Friday, and we closed the house on Saturday by adopting the address, which gave authority to the Prime Minister to advise the crown to declare war on our behalf. I ask any member of this house to-day, who was in parliament then, if he will rise in his seat now and say that if the Prime Minister had suggested conscription at that time we could have finished that debate in time for the declaration of war by Canada on Sunday. There is not a member of this house who does not know that, if we had talked of conscription then,, that debate would have gone on interminably.
Speaking of leadership, I want to ask hon. members what would have been the position of Canada in the eyes of the world, if through lack of leadership the Prime Minister had permitted this country to pass that fateful week-end without the declaration of war. Talk about what is being said to-day! He would have been eternally damned, and he would have deserved it if he had allowed that to happen.
Continuing then with the question of leadership, I would ask you to let your minds go back again. There is without question one man who has captured the imagination of the world to a greater extent than any other man in history, whether in times of emergency or in times of peace. That man is Winston Churchill, the Prim^ Minister of Great Britain. But I ask you this. Next to the things that Winston Churchill has done for us, next to what he has done in the marvellous encouragement which he gave the people of Great Britain after Dunkirk, is there anything that was greater, as a means of helping Great Britain and ourselves in the conduct of the war, than the magnificent

material help supplied to us by the people of the United States through the leadership of President Roosevelt?
I think I am safe in saying that, next to what was done by Churchill, the help that was given us by the United States has been greatest. Now, where did our own Prime Minister come in? Unfortunately, and I say this deliberately, when you listen to some people speaking, when you read some of the newspapers of the day, with reference to the question of leadership, you have to wonder, as I have often wondered, whether some of them hate Adolf Hitler most, or Mackenzie King. I say that deliberately. There are groups of men in this country who are anxious for total war against Germany; but they are anxious for total war against Germany only to the extent that it will not interfere with their total war against Mackenzie King. That is one of the truths of the situation which it is necessary for somebody to bring to public notice-and you will note, I say it is one of the truths of the situation.
I was speaking of Churchill and Roosevelt, and I spoke of the past slipping away so rapidly from us that we are inclined to forget it. To-day we talk about the Atlantic charter, which came from the conference between Churchill and Roosevelt, and we take for granted that help which went to Britain through the lease-lend agreement before the United States was actually in the war in consequence of attack from Japan. What brought about these things? To-day, I venture to say, even m the minds of many hon. members, there is only at best a dim recollection of Ogdensburg, the historic meeting between our Prime Minister and the President of the United States, which took place in August 1940. From that meeting at Ogdensburg have flowed all the things for which to-day the people of the allied nations are thanking President Roosevelt and the people of the United States; and if it had not been for the leadership of our own Canadian Prime Minister, there would have been no Ogdensburg. The lease-lend agreement would never have become an accomplished fact, the meeting between Churchill and Roosevelt would not have taken place, the Atlantic charter would still be a dream of some of us, the aid that has gone since then to Russia would not have been sent. And every part of that is attributable to the man who sits here to-day as leader of this government.
I come from the province of British Columbia, and many who sit here know that in northern Alberta, in northern British Columbia and in the Yukon, there has been constructed a series of airports designed to protect

The Address-Mr. Turgeon
western Canada-both British Columbia and Alberta-against attack from Japan across Alaska or the waters surrounding Alaska, and the Yukon territory. I will say more about that later. But who in this house forgets that the hon. member who then occupied the seat of the Leader of the Opposition, as soon as war was declared, rose in his place, properly so, and asked for some protection against air attack or attack in any other form across Hudson bay. You do not hear much of that to-day. Why not? We have our airports in western Canada, constructed or largely under construction, to protect us from attack from the west. The reason you do not hear much demand to-day for further protection against attack across Hudson bay is that United States troops joined in the occupation of Iceland.
Again I ask you, if the right hon. the Prime Minister of Canada had not given to the President and the people of the United States that inspiration which was the foundation of the leadership given us by that president, would there have been an occupation of Iceland by the troops of the United States? There is not a member of this house who will rise and say that he does not see a direct connection between Ogdensburg and the occupation of Iceland by United States soldiers.
There is nobody in this house or outside who will not see in the occupation of Iceland a direct connection with the winning of the battle of the Atlantic. Talk about leadership! What could have been better either for Great Britain or for Canada-and especially for us in Canada-than to save ourselves from defeat in the battle of the Atlantic? That perhaps has been the greatest thing that has yet been done since war was declared in September, 1939. And the saving of the battle of the Atlantic is traceable directly back to the meeting between the Canadian Prime Minister and the President of the United States at Ogdensburg; there is no doubt whatever about that.
I said, Mr. Speaker, I was going to support the plebiscite, and that I was prepared to accept whatever measure of compulsory service may be deemed necessary from time to time by our competent authorities, both civil and military. I spoke of our attitude towards leadership. I have made recommendations to this government which have not been carried out. But am I to rise up and say that because my recommendations were not accepted I am opposed to the government and do not believe in their leadership? What right have I to say that? Yet I have as much right-though none at all-as any other citizen of Canada or any hon. member of this house. But I should
be foolish if I thought every recommendation made by me must be accepted, otherwise I would consider it lack of leadership.
On the day on which Japan made her attack in the south Pacific I telegraphed the Prime Minister of Canada as follows:
As member of Commons House of Parliament I strongly recommend that Canadian government take all possible action against Japan through executive authority without awaiting special session of parliament. I also urge that your government take favourable action upon my previous recommendations, first that ministry for war be created and secondly that National Mobilization Act be extended to include military service in any part of western hemisphere and in Siberia and that further extensions be considered from time to time as circumstances warrant.
That recommendation has not been carried out, but I sincerely hope that in time it will be carried out. In the meantime I am accepting the leadership that says "the time has not come to accept your recommendations." I made that recommendation some considerable time before Japan entered the war; I wanted the National Resources Mobilization Act extended in that manner, first, because I thought it would be of general help, and secondly, because I could see, as every hon. member in this house could see, the coming of war with Japan.
We in British Columbia and those who come from Alberta-the people of these two provinces particularly-are in a dangerous position. I am not so much afraid of a direct attack, unless it be of a sporadic nature, against Vancouver and Esquimalt, as I am of positively planned attack across Alaska or over the Aleutian islands. If I may be permitted to bring to your attention, Sir, the geographic situation of the western coast of Canada, it will be seen that the Pacific coast does not run, as people generally in the east think it does, north and south, but northwesterly. The Yukon and Alaska are considerably west of Vancouver and Victoria, and just across the straits from Alaska are islands leading to the Asiatic mainland, Siberia and Manchukuo, and to Japan. Therefore I say it is our supreme duty to make it certain that we have every possible line of defence available for the Pacific coast.

speechtext: What about the military road?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am coming to that. I have suggested-and I know this could not be carried out by us alone even if our own civil authority thought it wise-that Canada and the United States should thoroughly train and arm a large force of troops prepared to step into Siberia the moment Russia and Japan become entangled. Because I am

The Address-Mr. Turgeon

warning the government-I do not have to; for we are represented here by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) who naturally has given this same warning-I am warning them again that from the moment Russia and Japan become embroiled that moment will see Japan occupying bases in Siberia and Manchukuo, which are only minutes of time, not hours, distant from Alaska-the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Black) knows that-only an hour or two from northern British Columbia, and only four or five hours at the most from Edmonton and Prince George and Vancouver. Incidentally in 1939 when Japan was making her good-will flight to the United States the plane flew around over the town of Prince George, where there is now one of these protective airports, spoke by radio to the then airport, asked for directions and came right down over Cariboo country and across the city of Vancouver and on to her destination in the United States. That was the line they followed.
Now may I say a word about criticism. I read a speech made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) the other day. I have the quotation here but I do not need to turn it up. He criticized this government because we did not have an air force available immediately to take its stand on the Pacific ocean for the protection of British Columbia. The hon. member knows that we have not the air force ready.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. member had better read my speech again, because I did not mention that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We have not got it ready because every available airman and every available aeroplane has been dispatched to Great Britain, which in the conditions that then existed was the proper thing to do. No hon. member of this house will criticize the government for having done it. I do not want the people of British Columbia to be needlessly alarmed, and I am sorry for another statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver South, for whom I have-I do not need to tell him, but I am telling the house because of him-a very high personal regard. I refer to a statement about the command on the Pacific coast. I feel certain that our military chiefs know what they are doing, and I think if any hon. member of this house is doubtful of the capacity or the efficiency of any officer commanding it is his duty first to consult the higher military authorities in order to make certain that his doubts are correct before he help create panic among people who know they may soon be attacked

by public expressions of doubts about the capacity of the men in our military command.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Certainly,

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does he believe in a triple command on the Pacific coast such as there is at the present time?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What I was talking about then was not what my friend said about the triple command but what he said about the man who is actually general officer commanding in chief on the Pacific. I can mention names; I was thinking of General Alexander, as the hon. member was.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How does the hon. member know whom I was thinking of?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: As far as the Pacific command is concerned-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
He should be supreme
commander, shouldn't he?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
All right, but is the hon. member going to blame the military authorities in Canada if through the whole military world it is the custom that there is an army command, a naval command, and now an air force command? I am convinced that there should be a supreme commander. I have not discussed the matter with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), but I have an idea that he will deal with this question himself. Just the same I feel positive that every possible means of coordination has been carried out, so that when the general officer commanding the Pacific command gives an order, that order will be carried out by every branch of the armed forces. If that is not so, the minister will correct me when he dteals with the matter in this house.
A few moments ago someone asked me about the military aspect. Well, I have spoken of the danger of attack from the north and northwest, and of the airports that have been constructed in that part of the country. I am not a military man, but I feel that Prince Rupert should be made a joint naval base by the United States and Canada. It would be presumptuous for me to say that this must be done, but I believe it should be done. I believe that the projected road from Prince Rupert to Prince George should be built by this government immediately, without asking the provincial government to contribute one cent toward the cost. I believe that to be a military road, the cost of which should be borne by this government. I believe the airport at Prince George should be connected by road with the airport at Edmonton. Again,

The Address-Mr. Turgeon
speaking from a military rather than a peacetime point of view, I believe an alternative route should be constructed between Vancouver and Edmonton, taking advantage of what is called the Blue River highway; and I believe the whole line of airports north and east of the Rocky mountains should be connected by highway with Edmonton. Those are my recommendations to the government with regard to highway communication in that great northwestern area of Canada which, make no mistake about it, is apt to be attacked.
Thinking again in terms of conscription, and this plebiscite, I remember that in his very good speech a few days ago the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), speaking of Australia, at page 21 of Hansard for this year, used these words, with which I quite agree:
Every able-bodied man in Australia has been called to the colours. I pray to God that it is not too late. I am afraid that it may be; for how can these men be trained in time for the defence of their shores, men who have never had previous training?
Apparently my mind likes to go back to the immediate past, for when I heard those words I remembered when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), then Minister of National War Services, returned from England, where he saw devastation in the extreme. He spoke in this house, and again on the radio, demanding that more men be trained, and suggesting that industry should be able to carry on without insisting that its employees be exempt from such training. I remembered the uproar that followed. The leader of the opposition condemned the minister for making that statement, and other hon. members did the same thing. We were told that the minister was making threats against the patriotic captains of industry; that he was going to upset the whole industrial programme; that there was no need to train more men, but that the greater need was in industry itself.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I never said anything of the sort.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Naturally I accept the hon. gentleman's word without question, but I should like to be quite clear. Is he saying that he offered no objection to the statement made by the then Minister of National War Services?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I criticized the statement of the Minister of National War Services, but on no occasion have I ever said that there was no necessity for trained men.
I have tried to hammer that into the minds of the Canadian public and of members of this house since the day I took my seat here.
44561-17$

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I had in mind particularly what appeared in the Ottawa Journal, but the hon. member did denounce the minister at that time. My very good friend the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) had spoken of the matter before the leader of the opposition rose. The hon. member for Parkdale, if I might quote him from memory, said he was shocked1 at the statement made by the minister, and later the leader of the opposition rose in his place and joined in the condemnation of the then Minister of National War Services because of the statement he had made. There is no question about that; and now I say that the very newspapers which are condemning the Prime Minister to-day are those which a-short time ago said that industry should come first.
I have before me two resolutions passed by great organizations of returned soldiers. I refer to these organizations not only because they are great, not only because they both create and express public opinion, but also because throughout this time of stress, particularly during the period when we were working by means of voluntary effort, this country received its greatest support from the men who gave their services in the last war, and their dependents. It seems to be an instinct of nature that makes us love most that for which we have suffered most; perhaps that is why, since the beginning of this war, we have been given more assistance by the returned soldiers than by any other group of men or women in the country. One of the resolutions to which I referred was passed by the Canadian Legion, the other by the Army and Navy Veterans' Association in Canada. Perhaps I may be permitted to put on record first the resolution passed by the army and navy veterans,, because I happen to be a member of that organization. This resolution was passed at Toronto on December 1, which, it will be noted, was before this government announced its intention to hold a plebiscite on the question of compulsory service or conscription. Here is the final paragraph of the resolution:
Be it therefore resolved that the Army and Navy Veterans Association in Canada in dominion convention assembled places itself on record as being in favour of some form of compulsory selective service for all men between the ages of twenty-one and forty, such service to embrace not only the armed forces, but all branches of the war effort.
And be it further resolved that the government of Canada, through its Prime Minister, be advised of this resolution and be requested to institute some form of compulsory selective service, or in the alternative to obtain the opinion of the people of Canada on the matter by means of a plebiscite at the earliest opportunity.
The Address-Mr. Turgeon

Here is the recommendation of the Canadian Legion, or that part of it which is pertinent:
Canada should bring about the complete and scientific mobilization, organization and utilization of all our resources in such manner that our country may be geared to produce essential foods and munitions and to wage war to a maximum capacity.
I say without hesitation or doubt in my own mind that I am completely in favour of those two resolutions. I am completely in favour of them personally as a citizen of Canada. But as a member of parliament I cannot blind myself to the fact that if, as I pointed out a while ago, this government had previously indulged or were now to indulge in immediate conscription of men for overseas service, without dealing with other things, such action would retard rather than advance our war effort.
I see some of my hon. friends smiling, and I know what they are thinking about. I say with the greatest respect that naturally they are thinking, first, that I am wrong. They are thinking, as some of them have lately made themselves believe, that the taking of this plebiscite is the reason there is discord. The taking of the plebiscite is not the cause of the discord at all. The cause of the discord is the discontent, the terrible discontent, of those men who are making the agitation. I ask any hon. member if he is prepared to rise in his seat and say that a government motion to-day for conscription of men for overseas, without dealing with all the other things which are generally meant when you speak of the subject of wealth, would pass the house any quicker and with any less discussion or discord than it will take to pass the plebiscite against which they are objecting.
Every hon. member knows that a motion of that kind would smash this house. It would be discussed through amendment and subamendment for weeks and weeks, and perhaps would not pass at all. What about delay?

this, that if the leader of the opposition will rise in his place and officially pledge his party to the total conscription of wealth-

I thank the house for
the privilege. I shall not detain hon. members very long. I was going to speak of other things which in themselves are contentious, but since I have the unanimous consent of the house to continue with my closing observations I will leave all further contentious matter aside.
I was speaking about delay and discord. In connection with delay I was going to quote only one sentence from a speech made by the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen in 1925. This was the speech in which he made his famous suggestion that there should be no declaration of war without a general election. With the courtesy of the house, 'I should like to deal with that. He said:
This would contribute to the unity of our country in the months to come, and would enable us best to do our duty. It would not mean delay.
That was the sentence I wanted to leave with the house in that connection.

Mr. Speaker, I express my thanks to you, and through you to hon. members, for this courtesy which for the first time has been tendered to me. May I conclude with an expression of friendliness. We have been told that discord would follow from this plebiscite. Let me give hon. members a'little personal experience. The other day my old friend, the former chief government whip, the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Gray) spoke, and took a course quite different from mine. If any hon. member thinks that the friendship which exists between him and me is going to be impaired because of that difference of opinion in connection with the plebiscite, then that hon. member is foolishly wrong, because it is not.
In closing I should like to leave a simple message from the grave-and I give this not only to the people of Ontario and of other English-speaking parts of Canada, but also, and particularly, to the people of Quebec who, naturally, are ill at ease because of what might be done in connection with the further prosecution of the war. I was honoured and privileged to enjoy an hour and a half with Sir Wilfrid Laurier only six weeks before he died. He spoke of his approaching death, his passing to the land beyond, and as he spoke, tears welled in his eyes. We had been referring to the conscription issue of 1917, and to the men who had left the Liberal party and joined the Union government. He said to me, "Some of my colleagues are angry with me because I did not become bitter against those who left us." He continued, "Turgeon, I can speak to you; you are younger than I. There is no greater blessing in life than that of forgiving-not that of being forgiven." With that impetuosity which goes with lack of experience and lack of knowledge of fundamentals, I blurted out, "Sir Wilfrid, that is all right; it may apply to those who left us with sincerity; but it does not apply to those who left us from ulterior motives." He said, "Turgeon, do not forget that those who left us sincerely require no forgiveness, neither from you nor from me. If you wish to taste that which I tell you is the greatest joy in life, the act of forgiving, then there is nothing left but to forgive those who left us from what you are pleased to call ulterior motives."

The hon. member always holds the attention of the house, because he speaks so fervently in that language which is not his native tongue. The hon. member made special reference to the part the Prime Minister is playing in the war-bringing the United States into it, so to speak. He referred to the Ogdensburg agreement and to various measures passed by the United States government. You would almost think from his remarks that the Prime Minister of Canada was directing the war effort of the United States. I am just wondering what the President of the United States thinks of the latest action of this government in asking for a plebiscite to release the Prime Minister from certain of his pledges.
The hon. member also spoke of the battle of the Atlantic, and took credit to the Canadian government, in association with the United States, because that battle was going successfully in the matter of convoys and so forth. I wonder if the hon. gentleman ever heard of the British navy.

The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross), true to form, is beginning his interruptions early in the game. He has not been here very often during this session, but I see he is here now, and perhaps he will be good enough to sit and listen.
The speech from the throne usually sets out the legislative programme of the government, but the speech on this occasion is remarkable in that it mentions a plebiscite which the government wishes to submit to the people in order that it may be released of certain election pledges. I shall not take time to read the reference; it has already been put on Hansard, but I say that this action on the part of the government is making Canada appear ridiculous not only in the sight of our own people but in the eyes of our allies.
The Address-Mr. Perley

I wish to refer briefly to the last session of parliament. It was a lengthy session and was devoted almost wholly to war measures and other government measures, and rightly so. Private members' days were taken away so that the private members had no opportunity to introduce resolutions and discussions upon them. I think at this session private members' days should be restored. There are about 230 members of the house outside of the cabinet, and if private members had the privilege of introducing resolutions and! discussions, many constructive and helpful suggestions would be made to the government. I hope that that will be taken into consideration.
I am sure there is no member of this house who desires to discredit Canada's war effort. We do not belittle it. Far from it. I am prepared to say that I think Canada's war effort has been very substantial in many respects, perhaps even greater than some of us expected. We have been passing through trying times, and I am going to give the government credit for what they have done. Some, however, think that still more can be done. We boast in Canada of the morale of our people. We are going about many of our affairs as usual, and I think we should take up the challenge which the Right Hon. Winston Churchill gave from the very floor of this house when he said that the morale of the people will not produce guns and tanks and planes. It is men who are required for that, and it is men we want. We are facing a crisis which challenges us all. In due course I shall make further reference to that.
Hon. members will recall that at the time parliament was dissolved1 in January, 1940, after one day's sitting, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had a majority of over one hundred in this house, and there was no need for any election at that time. But the Prime Minister plunged us into an election; he came back with the very substantial majority which he has at the present time, and now after twenty-two months in office he brings forth this plebiscite to be submitted to the people to release him from certain pledges he claims to have given to the Canadian people in the last election campaign.
As I said, the government has a very substantial majority in this house. We all know that the war situation has become very much graver in recent months. We believe, and I think the majority of the Canadian people believe, that this is no time for a plebiscite, in view of the crisis facing Canada and the world. It would have been more courageous for the government to bring in a

resolution for the complete mobilization of all our resources in finance, industry and manpower, and I venture to say that such a resolution would have the almost unanimous support of this house and of the people of this country.
I wonder what our soldiers overseas think about this plebiscite. From my own little town of Wolseley, with a population of 830, sixty-four of our boys have gone overseas, and I have an invitation card on my desk to all the boys from Wolseley overseas to get together at the Beaver Club on March 15 next. I wonder what those boys overseas will think of the action of this government in submitting a plebiscite to the people and what they would think of us if we supported the submitting of a plebiscite to release the Prime Minister of his pledges with no understanding of what he will do afterwards. Outside of the man-power available in Canada there are no forces to support our boys overseas. I think I know where they stand, and they know where I stood during the election. They know that I stood for complete mobilization of all our resources, in man-power, wealth and industry, in order to support our boys overseas no matter in which theatre of war they might be engaged. If we fail to do that, we are breaking faith with them.
I said a few moments ago that I wondered what the President of the United States thinks of this plebiscite. The President of the United States received a majority at the last election, after he had given a pledge in the election campaign that no United States troops would be sent outside of that country. But when the war with Japan came, did the President of the United States ask for a plebiscite to release him from the pledge he had given? What did Chamberlain do? What was his record following Munich? Did he think he had a birthright at stake, as our Prime Minister says he has? I think that was a childish reference. The Prime Minister said that he was being asked "to sell his birthright for a mess of their pottage", referring to the opposition to the plebiscite in the press and among the public. But Churchill and Chamberlain did not ask for a plebiscite-and there you have the difference between statesmen and a politician.
One of the reasons advanced for the plebiscite is that it will preserve unity in Canada. The position I take is this. Surely there is not an honest-to-God Canadian citizen who does not want to win this war, and if there is going to be any disunity, we had better see just where those people are. We should know about them.

The Address-Mr. Perley
It has been stated in this chamber, I think rightly, that from time to time both parties have made mistakes. We have heard much about the period of 1914-1918 and the conscription issue of 1917. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, that is all under the bridge; we are dealing with the present situation. But in referring to that period mention has been made of certain charges to the effect that the government of that day was corrupt. I know that Right Hon. R. L. Borden "cleaned house" when there was corruption. I recall statements about old horses which were sold down in Nova Scotia, and so forth, but the Prime Minister of the day, as I have said, did a thorough housecleaning. I suggest that before hon. members on the government side make any more references to this subject, they start and clean house too; and if they want to know where to start, we over here can tell them of a few things.

I might commend to the Prime Minister the memorandum, referred to by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Boucher), presented by the Canadian Legion and the Navy League. I have a copy of it here. Why do they not give us the facts and let us discuss the matter here? The Prime Minister said in a statement that the conscription issue should be fought out on the floor of parliament. I wish to mention the voluntary enlistments in the constituency I represent. I referred briefly to the matter in my own home town. In the constituency of Qu'Appelle we have a record of which we are proud. In the matter of enlistments our constituency stands about as high as any in Canada. We have no industry other than agriculture, and I want to pay a tribute to the farmers who allowed their sons to go- young men who enlisted early in this, game, before there was any thought of a plebiscite. The sons of the farmers in the Qu'Appelle riding have done nobly, and great credit is due them. But the supply of farm help is greatly depleted. There should be some selective scheme of service under which every farmer and every man in western Canada would be in a better position to carry on. Some farmers are now in a very critical position with regard to labour. What we want is equality of sacrifice. A great many of our boys are fighting for $1.30 a day, yet we know that in other parts of Canada young men are getting as high as $7 and $8 a day. There are some from our district who have gone east and got jobs at that rate of wages. Such conditions do not represent equality of service or sacrifice.

There are two fronts' on which we are fighting, the economic and the military. On the economic front we have achieved much. I am ready to give credit in that respect to the government. Great quantities of munitions, materials, guns and tanks have been produced. But I am not satisfied: with what has taken place with respect to agriculture. It is playing a very important part but not getting a square deal. The agriculturists of the west are as loyal as any class in the country. They have made a great contribution; they have done their part up to date, and they will continue to play their part in the winning of this war, but they want a fair and reasonable degree of consideration. Western wheat has played a very important part in maintaining the volume of Canada's exports. After the war, if it is saved, and it must be saved, agriculture will play a greater part than almost any other industry in the rehabilitation of Canada. That is one reason why we want a fair deal and equal sacrifice, so that we shall be able to carry on. We want a parity of prices with the products of other industries which the farmer has to buy in order to carry on his business. After twenty-two and a half months, I think we should have what I would term a food production board to give direction. Represented on that board should be farmers and others, who would direct in the production of different commodities.
The Prime Minister has stated, quite correctly, that the wheat surplus will prove to be a great asset in the winning of the war. While the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), may have had a policy in 1940 to reduce wheat acreage, growing less wheat in order to win the war, when he came back from Britain in 1941 his first pronouncement in Canada, and in the west particularly, was to the effect that all this wheat would be needed and that even much better prices than we were receiving then would be obtainable. Why therefore is there a change of policy now? Why not have prices on a parity with other prices in order to give the farmer a chance?
In the last two or three days we have seen in Ottawa a delegation from western Canada numbering 430 strong. They represented
185,000	signers of the petition. Why did they come to Ottawa? They represent the pool of western Canada and practically every other industry or interest in the country that depends on farming-the merchants, the boards of trade, the municipalities, from the standpoint of taxation, and so on. They are representative of various organizations, and I know that hon. members who attended the banquet given

The Address-Mr. Perley
last night in the parliamentary restaurant, and who saw that vast crowd, must have been impressed by their appearance. They are a splendid lot of men. The Prime Minister at least paid them that tribute. They came here because on former occasions when they have sent delegations-and they have done so many times-those delegations have not been properly received and have not been given the fair consideration which is due them. In order, therefore, to put their case squarely before the government and the parliament of Canada they decided to send this large delegation of 430. There is no reason why they should not come here.
Some people have been a little critical of the delegation; they have asked why they should come here and spend all that money. May I point out that taking the subscriptions at twenty-four cents each, that is not very much from each subscriber, and I think the trip was coming to these men. They will appreciate their experience here, even though I cannot say they will go home satisfied with the reception they got yesterday. The Minister of Agriculture more or less tore their brief to pieces, and possibly they will go home a little disappointed. They have not received all that they were asking for. But they were eminently fair in the brief they presented. I have it here but I will not read it. It contains a good many figures, and I am not going to quote figures to-day. I will only speak generally on this occasion, because on a future occasion I shall put the case of the western farmers fully before the house and bring forward such figures as are necessary to substantiate the arguments that I will then advance.
I cannot see why they should not get proper consideration. Their brief asks for a better price, a dollar a bushel. I do not think that is unreasonable. It asks that the 1942 crop be segregated and kept by itself on a quota basis, if you like. That is not unreasonable. It asks that the present surplus, beginning with the 1941 crop, be kept as a reserve following the conclusion of the war or when it may be needed later on-and we know it will be needed. We know what is happening in Russia, where the great wheat-growing plains are being devastated. We know what has happened to their machinery of production. Very shortly they will need this surplus wheat. I have never been concerned about a great surplus of wheat, because we have seen wheat pile up in Canada and then disappear almost over night.
I might refer to another brief presented to the government to show that western Canada is unanimous in the demand for a dollar or
better for wheat. We have from the Northwest Line Elevators association a demand for $1.02 net or a parity price of $122. It is interesting to me to read this brief and to know that it has been presented to the government, because I can recall this organization's attitude to the farmers of western Canada, especially during the period from 1930 to 1935, when they were not very favourable to us in our effort to boost wheat prices. We did not get very much support from them. It is interesting to note now that that organization is asking for a little more than the pool, through their representation, are demanding. I was wondering if there was any significance at all in the fact that the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) has played an important part in that organization and is close to it now. I do hope the government will give consideration to at least one of these briefs and give the farmers a fair deal, a parity of prices.
In the brief presented by the pool organizations reference is made to Canada's national income and the fact that twenty per cent of the population of Canada is in the west, in the three prairie provinces, and receives only five per cent of that income. There is something wrong there, and their argument is sound. Many hon. members will forgive me if I make a personal reference to my own record, though the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) may resent it.
When I came to this house in 1930 I was imbued with one idea-that if with my wide experience in farming and also having been in the grain business for a number of years, I could not do something to help western Canada, and the farmers of western Canada particularly, my time would be wasted. Some of my time may have been wasted, but I have a clear conscience in this, that never have I failed to take advantage of every opportunity that has offered to put up a case for the western people. I regret that on many occasions I have failed to receive the support that I had expected when I sat for three sessions as the sole representative of the Conservative party from western Canada. Hardly a Liberal supported me, though Doctor Motherwell did. He supported suggestions I brought forward, and some of them were good, if I may be allowed to say' so. I am glad to say that that gentleman, with a great deal of experience in his favour, and having the welfare of Canada at heart, did see eye to eye with me. But in 1934 and 1935, when the wheat board act was being passed, I fought-I think I may use that word-to have certain clauses inserted. It

The Address-Mr. Perley

so happens that only one hon. member of this house was a member of the committee to which that bill was referred, the Minister of: National Defence (Mr. Ralston). I am sure hie would bear me out when I say that time after time I insisted that certain clauses be put into that bill, taking in coarse grains, providing for price-fixing by a board, and so on.
Again in 1936 hon. members know what happened when I moved certain resolutions. Again in 1938 I suggested the processing tax, suggested a long-term price of ninety cents, possibly a dollar a bushel. I was right then because it is proven now that had we had that we would have been in a much better position and it would not have cost the country as much as it has already.
I made representations from time to time for a reduction in freight rates. In 1940 I had a resolution on the order paper, a copy of which I hold in my hand, calling for at least 90-cent wheat and the processing tax. I have a resolution on the order paper now which I hope will be reached in due course, and at that time I shall give some figures to show that we should have consideration and have a parity price fixed not for one year

this fiddling with the price each year is no use, because a review of the history of the past and of the prices over a period of ten or fifteen years indicates clearly that we can have a price which is nearer parity than the present price.
The Minister of Agriculture, even in 1939, speaking in this house on May 5, on Bill No. 83, as reported at page 3647 of Hansard, quoted Professor Hope to prove that farmers should have an average price of 95 cents to give them a decent living. That 95 cents he agreed should be net to the farmer, which would be about $1.15 at Fort William. He has changed his mind somewhat since, but I have here a quotation showing that he agreed with Professor Hope when he said that the farmers in order to carry on and have a reasonably decent living should have 90 to 95 cents net on the farm. Conditions are worse now; there is even greater reason for it than there was then.
I have here a comparison of the cost of living on the farm and in the cities and towns, taken from the Economic Annalist. Taking 1913 as the base year, 147 items, products of industry that the farmer has to buy, stand now at 143. But wheat is 14 per cent less, at 50 cents, than it was that year taken as the base. To-day industry is working on cost

plus; we know what happened to labour, increased wages and a cost of living bonus; but the farmers are still expected to produce at less than cost.

I suggest that the government consider adding a processing tax to a fair price; that they consider saving storage that they are paying to-day that they should not be paying to the grain companies, in terminals, annexes and in box cars-that is something I protested against; the average farmer in western Canada does not realize that he is paying for storage on a certain amount of his wheat in box cars; that they save interest by rebating the storage or making it possible for the farmers to store their grain on their own farms. What better asset could a farmer have than a thousand bushels of wheat in a bin secure on his own farm, on which he could realize sooner or later? It would be a splendid thing if the money paid by the government, some $20,000,000 for storage in other places, were to go back to the farmer. It would also result in a considerable saving in interest if the grain were stored on the farms rather than go to the market where it has to be paid for with consequent interest charge.
This is a national emergency, a national crisis that we are facing. This surplus will be needed, I am not worried about that. The government is financing purchases of food for Britain-cheese, bacon, butter, eggs, and so forth. I am not criticizing that at all, but I say they should go further and finance the purchase of wheat and deliver it to Britain at a fair price. That would be a splendid thing; it could come under that splendid offer made the other day by the Prime Minister to give a billion dollars or more to Great Britain.
I am going to support the amendment. It is far-reaching; it calls for complete mobilization of man-power, wealth, resources, industry and everything in Canada in order that we may have a complete war effort in any theatre of war. I trust, however, that the government will take into consideration the suggestions of the pool delegation. Their case was presented in a moderate way; they were fair and their representations deserve consideration. I believe the Minister of Agriculture is meeting with them now. In fact

The Address-Mr. Wright
he sent me a note just before I started to speak, saying he regretted he had to attend that meeting. Well, I regret it too, because I wish he had heard a few of the things I have had to say. However, relief assistance and marketing are two different problems and must be considered from different angles.
All we want is a long range policy which will give the farmers the security and parity of prices which will bring them into their own once again. I trust the government will be courageous. I trust that the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) will make an announcement within the next few days-it would be splendid if they could make it while the delegation is here-to assure these men before they return to the west as to what is going to happen next spring, so that they can know what is to be the policy with respect to acreage reduction and what payments they will get for the 1942 crop, and so they can go home ready to prepare for the spring work with some heart. I hope they will get favourable consideration, and I think an announcement should be made at once.
I have a resolution on the order paper that I hope will be reached in due course. I shall then be glad to present figures to show that the case presented by the pools is fair and reasonable.

I did not have the privilege of hearing the addresses of the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, but from the many compliments which I have heard from all parts of the house I realize that they made their usual able contribution to the discussions of this parliament.
It is not my intention to-day to try to deal with the many problems which are opened up by the speech from the throne, but rather to confine my remarks to one or two which I believe to be of paramount importance at this time and which should be dealt with without delay if our war effort is not to be seriously impeded.
First I should like to deal with the matter of the plebiscite, and secondly to say something concerning agricultural production in this country as related to our war effort.
With regard to the plebiscite, in many of the speeches in this house I think there has been too much emotion and not enough appeal to reason. It seems to me that the less we raise sectional differences and strife in this country at this time, the better it is going to be for the country as a whole. I do not agree with the idea of a plebiscite. I think 44561-18*
this parliament was elected during war time to carry on this war to a successful conclusion. In my own constituency some of my best friends came to me after the last election and said they had voted against me and for the government because they believed in a strong government that could carry on the war effort. I wonder what they are thinking to-day. I believe if the Prime Minister had come to parliament, placed all the facts before it and asked to be released from the commitments which were made by hon. members on all sides with regard to conscription, this parliament would have given him that release and accepted the responsibility.
After all, when we were sent here to Ottawa we assumed certain responsibilities, and I think we should be prepared to carry them out. I believe the ordinary man on the street to-daj is saying, "What are those fellows doing down there? Why don't they get on with the job? That is what we sent them there to do." I believe the sooner we do that the better it will be for Canada. I freely admit that this would have been a serious responsibility to assume, but I think most of us would have been prepared to go back to our constituents and defend our action. That procedure could have been carried through very quickly and with a minimum of expense. Various estimates have been made as to what this plebiscite may cost. In my view the greatest expense will be the time and labour that will be involved. It is not the money itself but the effort, the wasted energy, which might be employed to better advantage at this time.
I should like to deal with the three suggestions before the house at the moment. The government say, "We have already mobilized wealth and industry in this country. We have conscripted men for home service, and now we are asking you to release us from our promise not to conscript men for overseas service." I have no patience with those who go round the country belittling our war effort. Let no one be mistaken; we in Canada have made and are making a very valuable contribution to the carrying on of this war. The statement made in this house by the Prime Minister proves that. But I do not think any hon. member can state honestly that we have made our maximum effort, that we have used every dollar, every man and every woman to the greatest possible extent. Only when we have done that can we say that we have a total war effort. The government have conscripted men for home service, but as yet they have not conscripted wealth or industry; they have merely organized them. It is true that we
The Address-Mr. Wright

have high taxation, but as yet that taxation is far from being confiscatory. I believe we should measure our taxation in this way: that we should take in taxes in this country all income which enables any person to employ, either directly or indirectly, the services of any man or woman to do for him something which he is physically able to do for himself. When that point is reached I think we will find a great reservoir of labour and money made available in this country.
Let us look at the distribution of the last war loan, as set forth by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). The total number of subscriptions was 968,259, and the amount subscribed $836,820,250. Subscriptions of $50 and $100 numbered 661,282, or 68-3 per cent of the total number of subscriptions. The amount subscribed in this way was $45,302,650, or 5'4 per cent of the total. Subscriptions of from $50 to $500 numbered 861,046, or 88-9 per cent of the total number. The amount subscribed in this way was $115,300,950, or 13-7 per cent of the total amount. In other words 68-3 per cent of the subscribers invested only 5-4 per cent of the total amount, while 88-9 per cent bought only 13-7 per cent of the total loan. In other words 11-1 per cent of the subscribers took S6-3 per cent of the total loan. This shows those who were able to subscribe to that war loan.
I wonder what the men serving in our army, navy and air force are going to say when they return to Canada and find this situation. Are they going to be satisfied, when the war is over, to find that a small percentage of the people of this country will be able to sit back, clip coupons, and through those coupons, demand the services of the men who fought to make those coupons worth the paper on which they were written?

speechtext: If the hon. member would permit an interruption, I believe there is one point which should not be overlooked. Included in that smaller percentage of subscribers were several large insurance companies which invested the funds of a very large number of people.
