speechtext:
I quite agree, but even taking that into consideration I believe I am more than fair in saying that less than thirty per cent of those subscribing took more than seventy per cent of the last war loan.
I believe the sooner we in this house take a more realistic view of what is happening in Canada to-day, the less trouble we are likely to have in the post-war period. Only when we have conscription of accumulated wealth and industry, as well as of man-power, shall we have a total war effort. Let us take two

men who started out thirty years ago. The one man raised a family; the other did not. To-day we say to the man who has three sons, under our selective service system-and I believe in selective service-that his boys must serve where they can make their greatest contribution. To one we say, "You must serve in the army;" to another we say, "You must serve in the air force," and we allow the third to remain at home. What do we say to the man who did not raise a family and who, perhaps partly because of that fact and partly through fortuitous circumstances, was able to accumulate a certain amount of this world's goods? Do we say to him that he must give his money to the government? No; we institute expensive war loan drives and advertising campaigns to coax it out of him. This is entirely unnecessary. We should conscript wealth as well as the young men of the country. If we have compulsory service, it is necessary that we have compulsory interest-free loans, levied according to ability to subscribe.
Let us now consider the amendment moved by the Conservative opposition. It reads, in part:
This house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have not seen fit to recommend to parliament without delay additional measures designed to
(a)	completely mobilize the wealth and material resources and, on a selective basis, the full man and woman power of the nation, to the end that the nation may wage total war in any theatre of war;
(b)	supply the imperative needs of agriculture, industry, and the fighting forces of the nation; and
(c)	prepare for the post-war period.
This sounds very good. I could support that amendment myself if I were sure just what is meant. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated the other day that the substance of the amendment and that of the amendment to the amendment moved by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation were practically the same. I am afraid he was not using his usual keen sense of perception, otherwise he would not have made that statement.
To begin with, to mobilize means to organize. To conscript means to control and to operate. There is a vast difference between organizing an industry to produce as efficiently as possible, but for a profit, and controlling and operating that industry to produce as efficiently as possible, without profit, and for the state. That is the difference between the amendment moved by the Conservative party and the amendment to the amendment proposed by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. The hon. member for Lake Centre said the only difference was in the

The Address-Mr. Wright
method. As I said before, I do not agree with the method being used in connection with the plebiscite. I believe the question being asked is not a fair one. We believe that along with that question there should be another one, as outlined in our amendment.
First let us consider the mobilization of wealth and industry. The government states that it has already done that, and I have not heard one of the leaders of the Conservative party state publicly that he would go farther in that respect. In fact I have seen reports of speeches by Right Hon. Mr. Meighen in which he has stated that we have gone too far. The present leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) has stated in the house that he believes the excess profits tax is as high as it should be at the present time. He objected to many aspects of the succession duties tax. Yet they do not believe that we have gone far enough in the mobilization or, should I say, regimentation of labour, and the conscription of man-power. With regard to the second and third proposals may I say that I am in entire agreement.
Let us now consider the amendment to the amendment moved by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. It states:
This house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have used the sweeping powers conferred by the National Resources Mobilization Act mainly for the conscription of men for home defence, and in the opinion of this house no total effort adequate to meet the present needs of the war, domestic problems and the preparation for post-war conditions is possible without total mobilization of wealth, industry and finance, as well as human resources.
Therefore this house respectfully requests that the forthcoming plebiscite should seek the support of the people of Canada for the complete and effective conscription of war industries, accumulated wealth and financial institutions, at the same time and on the same basis of sacrifice as the suggested extension of the conscription of man-power.
There is no pussyfooting about that. We say, in effect, that we are realists. This is a total war, and the way to meet total war is by total effort. Let us put everything we have into the conflict-every dollar, every factory, every resource, every man and every woman, on an equal footing, at the same time and on the same basis of sacrifice, without hesitation and without quibbling. And when the war is over and victory won, let us start on an equal footing to build a better Canada, a better and saner world to live in. That is what the people of Canada want, and that is what the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation stands for.
We do not believe that when this war is over any individual or group of individuals, through holding accumulations of war bonds,
or by owning the factories and natural resources of this country, should be able to say to the people of Canada, "You must work for us. We own the tools with which you must work, the materials you must use. We control the tokens you must use to provide yourselves with the necessities of life. You must pay tribute to us."
For a short time I should like to deal with the matter of agriculture. Speaking in this debate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is reported to have said this, at page 34 of Hansard:
A vital aspect of Canada's war effort is our contribution to the food supply of Great Britain. This contribution has grown steadily in importance. Britain cannot feed herself, and her own great and growing armed forces. Still less can she feed the ever-increasing numbers of men we are sending from Canada to add to her armed strength. In the present war, unlike the last, her sources of food, on the continent of Europe have all been closed off by enemy occupation. Canada is the nearest source of food deft open. Without our food the people of Britain might starve. Without our food the Canadian army in Britain would be a handicap instead of a help. In a literal sense the very lives of the British people and our own armed forces overseas depend upon the exertions of Canadian farmers and fishermen. In prosecuting the war, theirs is no secondary role. As time goes on, the demands upon Canada for supplies of food for the allied forces and, later, for the peoples of the now subjugated countries are certain to increase.
I would call particular attention to these last two sentences:
I have mentioned food production separately because I doubt whether the country is fully aware of the vital importance of food regarded as a munition of war. Otherwise, it might well have been included as a phase of the productive aspect of our total effort.
Whose responsibility is it that it has not been included as a phase of the productive aspect of our total war effort? Whose responsibility is it that Canada is not aware of the vital importance of food, regarded as a munition of war? We have in the government a Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) who is in charge of publicity. If the country is not aware of the importance of food in our total war effort, then it is the responsibility of the government to make it aware of that fact. Knowing all the facts, why is it that the government has not made the production of food a phase of our total war effort?
Every hon. member who has been in Great Britain has stated that Great Britain needs all the concentrated foodstuffs we can produce. Nevertheless for the last two years the government has continued to treat agriculture as an industry of secondary importance. It has by economic pressure deprived agricul-
The Address-Mr. Wright

ture of its labour, and has increased the cost of the tools it must use to produce. We have not reached the maximum of our possible production in Canada, but I believe we have reached the limit of our present possible production, unless we are to supply either more labour or better tools with which the farmers may produce.
We have been asked for more dairy products. The only way in which we can have more dairy products is to pay a price for them which will enable the farmers to compete in the market for the available labour, and also to provide the necessary laboursaving devices. When the government wants more munitions, more guns, more aeroplanes, more tanks or more clothing, it assists the manufacturers to re-tool their plants and to produce those commodities as effectively and economically as possible. All agriculture asks is similar treatment.
During the past war there was a demand for wheat. Large areas in western Canada which never should have been broken up were put under cultivation. Farmers under the stimulus of increased prices bought equipment and assumed obligations which they could never fulfil. What guarantee has the farmer to-day that if he equips himself to produce dairy products, hogs and other requirements, he will not again be left holding the bag?
Industry has stated in no uncertain terms: If you want more plant or equipment than we can use in peace time, then the government must build it and we will operate it for you. This government and the British government have accordingly erected some 600 million dollars' worth of such plants. How much assistance has been given the farmer to construct new plant or equipment to produce food? How much, assistance is to be given him this year to see that he is able to procure Labour-saving machinery to replace the men going into the army and into industry? These are some of the questions the government must answer if they are to get greater production.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is asking the western farmer to grow more coarse grains. I will tell him -how he can get more coarse grains sown. Just guarantee to the farmer that he will receive the full cost of production, including depreciation, replacement and a fair return on capital investment. At the present time there is a maximum price on coarse grains but no minimum. Every farmer knows from sad experience over the past twenty-five years that if he grows a bumper crop of coarse grains this year and the speculative market is left open, the price

will go below the cost of production. What incentive, is there, then,	to increase
production?
If the government want greater production of coarse grains, all they have to do is to close the Winnipeg grain exchange, announce that the present maximum price will also be the minimum price and that the premium on malting barley will be increased to ten cents a bushel. If they do that, they will get greater production.
Last fall there was a demand for malting barley in the United States, and considerable quantities were being shipped. Then this government stopped the export, and immediately the price in this country dropped. The government stated that we needed for feeding purposes all the coarse grains we had in Canada. Anyone knows that wheat can be substituted for barley for feeding purposes, and we have plenty of wheat. The breweries are using large quantities of barley. They cannot substitute wheat. Did they bring pressure to bear on the government to stop the export so that they could: get cheaper barley? If there is a real shortage of barley for feeding purposes, would it not be better to use it to produce bacon for Britain rather than beer for ourselves? The speculative market, whatever may have been said in favour of it in peace time-and I do not think there was anything to be said in favour of it then-certainly in war time serves no good purpose. It only confuses and discourages the producer. We are told that the law of supply and demand controls our prices, but anyone who has followed prices in this country of agricultural products in particular knows quite well that that is not the situation. Let me give you an instance.
In July of last summer a neighbour of mine shipped two animals, a two-year-old heifer and a herd sire, to the Winnipeg market. For the heifer he received $8.25 per hundred pounds, and for the sire $6.50 per hundred. Six weeks later, another neighbour made a similar shipment. He received $8.20 per hundred pounds for the herd sire and S6.50 per hundred for the heifer. I am sure that the people of Canada had not changed' their eating habits during that short interval. The government to-day are the largest purchasers of a number of products, and the only basis there could be for assuming that the demand had changed would be that the government needed: more boloney to feed to the Canadian people through its propaganda department. How is the producer to know what are the requirements, with the market jumping in this manner?	.
We have had in Ottawa this week a large delegation from Saskatchewan to present to

the Address-Mr. Wright
the government what the farmers believe to be the just demands of western agriculture. Their demands have received the approval of the organized farmers in both Manitoba and Alberta and have been approved by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. They have also received the support of the towns and cities of the west. The requests of the farmers are moderate-the minimum, in their opinion, on which western agriculture can continue to produce. If the Prime Minister's statement, that food is needed and will be needed in increasing quantities, is correct, then I believe this government should see to it that necessary action is taken to give effect to their requests. I consider that there is something seriously wrong with our democracy when any section of this country finds it necessary to send such a delegation to Ottawa. Either we who represent them have failed to place their case fairly before the government, or the government, knowing the case, have refused to pay any heed to it. Surely the government knew of these conditions.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture both represent Saskatchewan constituencies. Last summer I attended in the Prime Minister's constituency a public meeting called for the purpose of protesting against the present price of wheat. The largest theatre in the city of Prince Albert could not hold the crowd, and hundreds stood on the street listening to the loud-speakers. The chairman of the board of trade, the mayor of the city, along with the reeves of the municipalities, stood on the platform and openly supported the demands which the present delegation are bringing to Ottawa. The farmers of Saskatchewan do not want to be paid treaty money; they want a price for their products that is equal to the cost of production. They would like to see the present Prairie Farm Assistance Act so amended that it will become a comprehensive crop insurance plan. After our experiences over the past twelve years in Saskatchewan, we realize that crop insurance must be a part of any plan for the rehabilitation of western Canada.
Three things I believe are essential if we are to get increased production: (1) a parity price;	(2) the labour situation must be
rectified, and (3) provision must be made for supplying up-to-date machinery and1 repairs at reasonable cost. If these things are done, I am sure that we can materially increase our present production of needed food.
First, as to the parity price, I would ask the Minister of Agriculture what formula was used in determining maximum prices for agricultural products. We know, according to the bureau of statistics, that over thirty-three
per cent of the population of Canada were engaged in agriculture in 1939 and that they received only eleven per cent of the national income that year. We also know that since the war our national income has probably doubled1, but agricultural income has not kept pace with this advance. Using as a base 100 in 1926, we find that grain products to-day stand at 57-9. Animal and dairy products have reached an approximate parity. There is certainly no equality in such a situation.
This government, instead of developing a balanced, equitable programme for agriculture during the war, has simply drifted along trying to deal with each separate situation as it arose. We have an agriculture committee of this house. The first time it was called together during the life of this parliament was when it was invited to the banquet of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture last Thursday. We enjoyed the banquet. We heard there a speech from Mr. Evans, chairman of the AAA farm programme in the United States, who outlined the comprehensive programme which they have adopted. They have been developing it for the last eight years. When war was declared last December, it found agriculture in the United States prepared to take its place in the war economy and do its full share on an equal basis with labour and industry. Agriculture in Canada asks similar treatment.
I would advise every hon. member who is interested in agriculture to-day to make a study of what they are doing in the United States. I am sure there are points in their programme which can be copied in Canada to our advantage. Their price is based on an equality with wages of labour and retail prices. In the United States to-day they have a guaranteed price of SI .17 a bushel for wheat, while they are able to buy their implements and tools of production at from fifteen to twenty-five per cent less than we can in Canada. They have an ever-normal granary programme whereby thirty per cent of the normal crop of non-perishable foods is kept in reserve. They have a land conservation programme and a comprehensive crop insurance plan.
Second, with regard to the labour situation in Canada, if we are to increase the present production of the foods we need for Great Britain, some form of selective service draft will have to be introduced immediately. I believe that we have drawn from the farms of Canada all the men that we can by our present methods without seriously affecting production. If it is essential that more be called, then we must make provision to replace them by other labour.
The Address-Mr. Wright

Now, just a word with regard to agricultural implements. Their price has for years been out of line with the price of agricultural products. The government have known this. It is ancient history. They appointed a commission, spent thousands of dollars, ascertained all the facts, and then took no action. I am not going to enter into a discussion of this matter this afternoon. I should like to point out a greater danger at this time. Last year it was becoming increasingly difficult for the farmers to get repairs for farm machinery. Unless the government see to it that companies make proper provision for this, I am afraid many of them may concentrate on the more lucrative production of war materials. Now is the time to take steps to prevent this. If we wait until the situation becomes acute next fall, it will be too late. I would ask the government to make the necessary investigations at once and to see that this situation does not develop.
I know the farmers of Canada; I have farmed in both eastern and western Canada. They are willing and anxious to do their share. They ask for no special privileges. They demand equality. Given that, they are prepared to make all the sacrifices which may be necessary to secure victory.

speechtext:
Like so many hon. members who have preceded me, I wish to take this opportunity of complimenting the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It is indeed fortunate that the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier) and the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) are men of superior intelligence and modesty, otherwise I fear that enlarged heads might require new hats, at a time when we are asked to limit our purchases as much as possible.
It is my desire to-day to plead with this house for tolerance and a better understanding in this great dominion of ours. Often, however, in attempting to be tolerant, one becomes impatient of those who are intolerant. This I shall attempt to the utmost of my ability to avoid.
We must all strive to understand that each section of Canada has its own particular problems. We have one of the longest and, thank God, the most friendly boundaries of any nation in the world. But the very fact that we have such a long boundary, stretching well over three thousand miles from the Atlantic to the Pacific, means that we have more than ordinary problems to face. In the maritimes they have difficulties which are peculiar to those three provinces. Quebec has its own difficulties. Ontario has questions which are of vital importance to that province.

We know that the three prairie provinces find themselves in a dilemma to-day chiefly as a result of world conditions affecting wheat. We know also that British Columbia is facing great difficulties. It is therefore, during time of war, more important than ever that we try to understand each other, that we bury our differences, that we comprehend Canada not in a narrow sectional way but as a nation as a whole. In that way we can overcome once and for all, for the duration of the war and, I hope, for all time, sectionalism and distrust.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has consecrated his life to the task of unifying the dominion, and up to the immediate present no other man has succeeded to the same extent that he has. When he assumed office in 1921 Canada was disunited and resentful, but through his indefatigable perseverance a degree of unity was approached such as this country had never known. Some weeks ago I was telephoned by a member of the committee of two hundred which was meeting in Toronto at the time with the alleged object of advancing Canada's war effort. I was asked if I favoured the policies advocated by this committee. I said in reply that if what they were after was national selective service with complete mobilization of all our man-power and. resources, I was heartily behind them', but that if it was only conscription of men for overseas service, I was diametrically opposed to that. Unfortunately, as time goes on, the only issue which appears to be advanced is that of conscription for overseas service. It is being used as a smoke-screen to hide all other Canadian achievements and problems.
Some had high hopes that with the second coming of George McCullagh and his two hundred prophets a great deal might come out of Canada. I said "some", not all of us, because all too many of us remember his leaderless-I beg pardon, Mr. Speaker-his Leadership league and how it evaporated into the mists.
More recently another voice a few blocks away from the office of the Globe and Mail has been heard not only across Ontario but throughout the length and breadth of Canada. I refer to the premier of Ontario, who has on several previous occasions tried to split the Liberal party, but who to-day is trying new and far more sinister tactics and, with his uncalled for, unjustifiable and contemptible remarks, is in danger of splitting Canada. Well do I remember when he referred to Ontario as the milch cow for the rest of Canada. I wonder how the other eight provinces felt about that. As a citizen of Ontario I did not feel happy about the remark. I remember sitting in this house when he

The Address-Mr. Fuljord
scuttled the dominion-provincial conference on the Sirois report, a little over a year ago. Whether one believed in the recommendations of that report or not is beside the question; the fact remains that these delegates were asked to stay when the report was thrown out and discuss any problems of vital importance concerning each province in the dominion in relation to the dominion as a whole, and this same man who sets himself up on a pedestal in Ontario would have nothing to do with it. Instead of listening to reason and trying to contribute something to the conference, he caught the first train back to Toronto in a huff.
To-day we see him in Welland, and I shall quote a few remarks of his as published in the Ottawa Citizen of this morning, Tuesday, February 3, 1942. I quote:
The premier criticized the federal government for what he said was a "policy of appeasement in every critical issue before and since the war began", termed the calling of the plebiscite a "criminal act" of reneging on the government's commitments and declared "this government at Ottawa has been a sham government."
Compare that with the remarks made by the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, probably one of the most outstanding men of to-day, leader of the British empire, when he said in this very house on December 30 last:
The contribution of Canada to the imperial war effort in troops, in ships, in aircraft, in food and in finance, has been magnificent.

speechtext: He was talking about the people of Canada, not the government.

speechtext:
But the government are
regulating the affairs of the people.

The
people are supplying the money and brains.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The people would not
have had an opportunity to make this contribution had it not been for the policies of the government. Whose opinion are the people generally of Canada to take, that of a little man in Toronto who desires more power than his mental capacity is equal to, or the opinion of the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the Right Hon. Winston Churchill?
I wish to quote some more remarks of the premier of Ontario.
The calling of the plebiscite, Mr. Hepburn said, was the "crowning instance" of the federal government's appeasement policy. . . . Mr. King had attempted to appease the west as well, Mr. Hepburn said. "To appease the west we speculated in wheat and the wheat board announced the other day that we had lost nearly $80,000,000 on our speculations. Then we bonused the west to grow wheat and after that we bonused the west not to grow wheat."
Does that sound like a man who is trying in this time of crisis to unify the country- pitting one section against the other. Further:
"The trouble is that we've been loaded down with a policy of appeasement", the premier declared.
He referred also to appeasing the province of Quebec-another jab at another province. I do not believe that even Mr. Hepburn's most intimate friends and associates are in sympathy with the stand he is taking to-day. He has let his party down; but worse, far worse, he has let his province and his country down.
At the beginning of my remarks I pleaded for tolerance, but there is one thing that no tolerant person can overlook or forgive, namely, betrayal and treachery; and that is what we see in the premier of Ontario to-day. To those sitting opposite, I should like to offer a word of advice regarding this political chameleon. At present he professes to back the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen; but let me read what he had to say at the nomination meeting at a by-election in the provincial riding of Hastings East, in the village of Madoc, on Thursday, December 2, 1936. I have no doubt the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) will remember that day. I remember it because, when Mr. Hepburn rose to speak, bedlam was let loose. I have never heard so many people shouting so loud in so many different veins, some boos and some cheers, but always to a general confusion such as one seldom sees anywhere. Allow me to read what Mr. Hepburn thought of Mr. Meighen on that day. This is reported by the Canadian Press and comes from the files of the Montreal Gazette. It is dated: Madoc, December 2:
Premier Hepburn, speaking here to-day in a joint debate with Conservative leader Rowe, reiterated Liberal charges made in the 1934 Ontario general election about Senator Arthur Meighen dealing in Ontario Power Service Corporation bonds while a member of the hydro commission.
"Meighen had $300,000 of these bonds" said the premier. "He violated his oath of office. He bought $90,000 more."
The reference to Mr. Meighen was made in the course of a criticism of administration of Colonel George Drew, former Ontario Securities' Commissioner.
I want hon. members to get this tie-up:
"During Drew's administration of his office there was more graft and corruption practised in Toronto than ever before," the premier said. First act of Colonel Drew's successor, he added, was to oust 91 "high pressure" stock salesmen from a Toronto hotel.
Colonel Drew, Conservative campaign director, sat on the platform and heard the premier
The Address-Mr. Fuljord

repeat last night's challenge that he get any responsible mining men to endorse the Drew administration of the commissioner's office.
"I telephoned Mr. MeCrea (Charles McCrea, former Ontario mines minister) _ to-day and he declined to comment," the premier said. "His very silence is its own condemnation of Drew."
Mr. Hepburn charged $12,000,000 had been taken from the Ontario investing public because Colonel Drew failed to act on information placed before him in connection with investment trusts with which Mr. Meighen allegedly was associated.
"Western shareholders asked Ontario to investigate manipulations by the trust and made charges of fraud," Mr. Hepburn said. Attorney-General Price sent the file to Drew who was being paid $10,000 a year. He reprimanded the shareholders publicly and said the matter was not in his jurisdiction.
"After that Meighen met Price and you can't tell me Drew didn't have his ear to the keyhole. The Tories stick together in milking the public. These custodians of justice-Drew, Price and honest George Henry (former premier) got together. They said, 'What will we do for little Arthur? He's in a bad way'. And they decided to buy Ontario Power Service bonds. Meighen was on the hydro commission and the commission took over at $18,000,000 bonds which had a market value of $6,000,000.

I hang my head in shame when I think that I was the chairman of the meeting that chose Mitchell F. Hepburn to lead the Liberal party in Ontario. I further hang my head in shame to think that I was a member in the Ontario legislature for three years and four months suffering the indignities imposed upon the private members of that body by the dictator of Ontario. I believe that the people of not only Ontario, but of all Canada, of the other eight provinces that he has insulted time and time again, will realize, once and for all, the calibre of man that he really is, and stop listening to his silly palaver.
The remarks of Mr. Hepburn regarding our Prime Minister are beneath contempt and an insult to the intelligence of the electorate of Canada. The Prime Minister has been spoken of as a coward. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that no man is a coward who can

withstand the tirades and insults emanating from certain sources in Toronto. He has conscientiously and courageously withstood those taunts from that section, taunts that are unwarranted, unnecessary and unbelievable. When the voice of the people is heard through the plebiscite, those hysterical screams and screeches will be drowned for now and for all time.
No one in this house, or, for that matter, in Canada, can help being thrilled when he reads of Australia and the deeds of her soldiers, sailors and Royal Australian Air Force, many of the latter of whom were trained in Canada under the empire training plan. History will acclaim for all time the bravery of Australian soldiers in Libya, Greece, Crete, and, more recently, Singapore. The defiance by Australian sailors of the enemy throughout the seven seas, and the exploits of her airmen over Germany and the conquered nations of Europe, over Libya, Singapore and the Dutch East Indies, and over the Japanese and British mandated islands in the south Pacific have covered them with glory.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has referred to the plebiscite as being un-British. But Australia had two referenda in the last war. I shall quote from Chambers' Encyclopedia the definitions of "plebiscite", "initiative" and "referendum":
A plebiscite is often used in Britain for an attempt to secure an expression of opinion on some special point of local interest by all the inhabitants of a district.
An initiative and referendum-the political institutions under which the people of a nation may initiate measures to be enacted by their own votes into laws.
The fundamental difference between the two is that a plebiscite allows a government to change acts or laws, whereas a referendum requires that the laws be changed'; but in principle they are very similar and in no sense can either be termed "un-British".
In this war Australia has no conscription for overseas service. South Africa has no conscription; India has no conscription, and the people of northern Ireland are just talking about it now. Is it not an insult to our sister dominions and other parts of the empire for us in this country to condemn the government of Canada for not introducing it here when it is not introduced generally elsewhere within the empire? Let us remember that every time a thrust is given this government, there is also given a thrust against the government of south Africa, northern Ireland, India and Australia.
Now that Australia's position is desperate, she is mobilizing her man-power up to the age of sixty for home defence.

I should like to suggest that even before the plebiscite, Canada begin total mobilization of man-power and resources. I know that this is under consideration, and I have no doubt that before many months have passed, it will be brought before the public in concrete form. We have heard from several hon. members from British Columbia of the danger in which the west coast finds itself, and we know that German submarines are operating off the Atlantic seaboard. I believe that before the coming of summer even greater dangers will assail us from the powers of evil. We must be prepared for any emergency. We must even accelerate our industrial and agricultural production. But, above all, we must be ready to meet, to the extent of our capacity, any and all demands made on us by the empire and the United Nations.
The outposts of the United States have been struck; Singapore and our sister dominions of New Zealand and Australia are in grave peril, and our own seacoast may be and can be invaded. We must, therefore, be ready to strike and strike hard. But this we cannot do unless Canada is united as never before. Let us, therefore, back this plebiscite to the limit of our ability-and I appeal to all parties in this respect-to assure the Prime Minister and the government that the voters of our dominion are fully conscious of the gravity of the situation. The Prime Minister, his ministers and supporters, must be released from a pledge made before the subjagation of Europe by Germany, before the entry of Italy into the war, and before that most treacherous of all attacks made by Japan in this most gigantic and horrible of all wars.

Will he go through with it, or will he just get the machinery for a plebiscite in shape and then, at the last moment, spring a general election? If he does that, the people of Canada will not only rebel; they will be
very much disappointed in the Prime Minister and the government. They want to know the reason for the delayed action. Why does the Prime Minister continue to play politics? Does he know something he is not telling the people? Will the plebiscite create unity or lunacy? That was asked me by a soldier. The other day I was speaking to a lady who has three sons in England. She said she did not think the mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, wives and sweethearts of the men in the armed forces would appreciate the fact that here in Canada we shall be marking crosses on plebiscite ballots while crosses are being raised over the graves of those brave men who are fighting for us.
Instead of taking a plebiscite, I wonder whether it would not contribute more to the unity of Canada, about which we hear so much, if the government raised the pay of the armed forces to a level equal or nearly equal to that of the men and women in our munitions plants. If that were done, I believe, after talking to a number of men working in those plants and also talking to soldiers, that there would be absolutely no need to talk about conscription because all the men needed could be got without it. They would sign up to fight in Canada or anywhere in the world they might be needed. At the present time they get SI.30 a day, with S20 a month deducted for their wives or mothers. Then, if a man from my city, for instance, wants to go home on twenty-four hour leave, it costs him $5.50 to go from Ottawa to Peterborough. The other night I picked up two air force boys at Port Hope. They had paid $5.50 for a ticket from Ottawa, and there they were left stranded, thirty miles from Peterborough. The rate seems to be the same whether they go to Port Hope or Peterborough, and there they were left with thirty miles to walk. One of these air force boys said that if the government paid the soldiers more money, eventually the government would get it all back again. The soldiers spend their money on train fare, for one thing, and the government owns the railway. Every time they buy anything the government gets part of the money in taxes, and those taxes are pyramided, what with the corporation tax, the excess profits tax, the sales tax and everything else. Certainly that money would come back to the government not once 'but perhaps twice over. The munitions worker gets a bonus, but the pay of the soldier has not been raised. The men and girls in the munitions factories believe they are getting something extra by way of the bonus, but in reality their purchasing power is not increased at all.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT OF REVEREND B. C. ECKERT WITH RESPECT TO CASUALTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the indulgence of the house, if I may have its unanimous consent, I should like to make a statement with regard to an item which appeared in a Toronto morning newspaper this morning respecting the report of an address made by
Hong Kong

Reverend B. C. Eckert, of London, at Welland. It has to do with casualties at Hong Kong, and I feel that it makes a rather serious charge. But what I am more concerned with is that I am afraid it will have the effect of seriously adding to the distress of those who are waiting for news from Hong Kong. I should like to make a statement with regard to it.
I have noted the statements said to have been made by the Reverend B. C. Eckert, as published in a report in a Toronto paper this morning. The report reads as follows:
The initial address was made by Reverend B. C. Eckert of London, who charged the King government with deliberately withholding the Hong Kong casualty lists until after the February 9 by-elections.
Ottawa knows them, and more are buried in the blood-stained soil of Hong Kong than are in Japanese prison camps.
The statement made by this reverend gentleman at W elland, to the effect that information regarding casualty lists was being deliberately withheld until after the February 9 by-election, is absolutely false.
I can state that no casualty lists have been received respecting the Canadian expeditionary force at Hong Kong except those which have already been published by the press.
Regarding the statement which directly implies that the number of dead exceeds the number of prisoners of war, the government has no information which would afford foundation for any such statement In view of the distress which this statement will cause, I have thought it advisable to give the house the following circumstances: We pressed the embassy at Chungking for information regarding Canadian troops from the reporter, MacDougall, who was reported to have escaped, and received a reply that casualties were difficult to estimate, particularly due to the fact that communications had ceased with the Royal Rifles, and the message then said:
Guess but only guess one-third of fighting strength killed, wounded or taken prisoners during fighting, remainder presumably taken prisoners on capitulation.
I consulted with the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Power) who, as the house knows, is personally and very intimately interested in this Hong Kong expedition, and we considered that what was emphasized as [DOT] being a pure guess was not the sort of speculation which ought to be given to the public, at least without further efforts to get something reasonably definite and reliable.
Since then we have been straining every nerve to get further information, and what 
we finally got yesterday was another message which had been sent to the War Office. It
stated:
Casualties whole British force Hong Kong "very rough guess 4,000 killed and wounded."
I may say that we estimate that the whole British force would number nearly 12.000. You will note that this message was even less informative to us than the previous one since it made no reference to Canadians, and it was also emphasized as a very rough guess.
I again consulted with the Associate Minister of National Defence, and we decided that no good purpose could be served in making public such unsatisfactory and inconclusive reports. Neither of these statements gave any particulars whatever; there would be neither definiteness nor reliability in the statements; they would give no genuine information to Canadians and might needlessly increase the distress and anxiety which is now being endured.
Even in view of the statement by the reverend gentleman, I have hesitated to give these uninformative and possibly misleading reports. However, his statement means in effect that more than half the force were killed. What basis he has for this I cannot imagine. We have nothing whatever to indicate any such situation. The guesses to which I have referred certainly do not.
But after consultation with my colleague we have decided that a statement of this kind made by a clergyman would, if left unanswered, only add to the terrific burden which the friends of those who were in the Hong Kong expedition are now bearing, and that is why I am now giving the house the substance of the indefinite messages, guesses though they are.
Actually, I am afraid we have erred too much in the direction of giving information without confirmation. As a result of this, in one deplorable case a cable which appeared to show an officer as killed proved, on our receiving further word, to give good ground for belief that this conclusion was incorrect.
I deplore deeply the occasion which has made it seem advisable to give the wholly incomplete and unverified surmises contained in these messages. Only a desire to counteract as far as possible the additional distress which will have been caused by the statement made by the reverend gentleman would have led me and my colleague to change the considered view which we arrived at that we were not justified in publishing these guesses without verification and where they might only increase needlessly the anxiety which we all share.

They should be placed in positions. They should not have to go hunting for them. The government should find places for them in industrial plants or elsewhere. It seems to be customary in this house for a member who rises to speak to compliment first of all the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and then for those on the opposing side to break his nose or black his eyes or to do something of that kind. I am not going to do that to-night. I reserve the right to break noses if necessary, but I am not extending compliments in that direction. I should like, however, to compliment the hon. member behind me, the member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka). I am not competent to pass judgment on the subject matter of the address he gave, but his presentation was excellent. As regards the people on whose behalf he spoke, I have only the highest commendation to offer, having lived among them and worked with them since coming to this country a number of years ago. I found them to be hard workers, people who have been doing their share to build up the country, and who have been playing their part in the effort to defeat the enemy overseas.
Let me now refer to the old age pensioners. We have heard a good deal in the past in this house and on the street, and we have read in the press, about the condition of our old age pensioners. The question was dealt with by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) on November 14 last. After giving a number of reasons why the government could not do anything for these people, either by way of a bonus or by an increase in their monthly pensions, he went on to say, as reported at page 4429 of Hansard of that date:
Indeed the government is prepared to consider going further than this. It believes that, for the reasons already outlined, it would be impossible to justify an increase in the maximum rate of pension payable if the whole cost were to be assumed by the dominion, and that such cases as appear to present immediate difficulties can be met by the provinces on the basis of established individual need. If, nevertheless, all, or substantially all the provinces should make representations to the dominion government in favour of some increase in the maximum amount of pension payable, the additional cost to be shared between the dominion and the provinces on the same basis as the present cost, I can assure the committee that the government will be prepared to give consideration to such representations.
I do not think it would be very hard for any of us, if we were inclined that way, to find reasons why old age pensioners should be given a cost of living bonus, or a permanent increase in the rate of pension. This legislation I believe went into effect away back in 1927. At that time the cost of living index stood at about 120; to-day it is close to 116;
[Mr G. K. Fraser.]
and the minister gives this as one reason why they are not entitled to a cost of living bonus. I would point out that in arriving at the cost of living index, quite a large number of items are taken into consideration, whereas in the old age pensioners' buying of supplies a very limited number are involved, and we find that the price of those goods which are purchased by old age pensioners has increased much more than the average
Then, again, I would say to the minister that if he wants to find excuses for giving something to the old age pensioners, he might look over the living allowance paid to some of our dollar-a-year men. That runs anywhere from $10 to $15 or, in some instances, more a day. Then, again, we find that others who are on very large salaries get up to $35 a day living allowance. That has happened in the past. Surely something along that line, although not that much, could be done for the old age pensioners. Some of our judges who give service for a certain number of years and are pensioned off get pensions ranging from $5,000 to $15,000 a year. This means that they have a pension of from $13.70 up to as high as $27.40 a day, and we were told not very long ago that this cannot be reduced. Perhaps that is because we have so many lawyers in parliament.
There is another group of pensioners, I would call them, not very far from here; I do not know what their qualifications are for their positions, but they are on the pension list. It is not called an old age pension or relief list, but they get a pension of almost $11 a day for life as well as other things that cost the country quite a lot of money. Perhaps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) could take some of these matters into consideration when again dealing with the question of cost of living bonus or increased pensions for old age pensioners.
I consider that this government and governments that have been in office in past years are responsible for the condition of many old age pensioners to-day, because these governments have passed and supported legislation which permitted exploiters in Canada to take advantage of and legally rob these people who to-day find themselves in need of old age pensions. Therefore I am of opinion it is now the duty of the government to take care of them in at least a reasonable manner.
In connection with that part of his statement in which the minister said that if all or a substantial number of the provinces want to do something about it, the government will give it consideration, I believe a start along this line has already been made by Alberta

The Address-Mr. Fair
and British Columbia; and I hope the other provinces will see that a start is made in the very near future and that this government will give it the consideration to which it is entitled.
We go on to another group of Canadians who, I believe, are also entitled to a cost of living bonus. I refer to our teachers all across the dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific. We have been told in the past that teachers are working for very low salaries, and that condition still exists to-day. I do not know whether hon. members all realize that we are entrusting the training and education of our children to these teachers for the greater part of the day during at least five days a week. We expect the teacher to live and dress respectably and when setting their rate of salary, seldom think of the many other duties for which the teacher is made responsible. In order to bring them up to the same level as some of our industrialists and civil servants who to-day are receiving a cost of living bonus-about which I am not complaining-I think we should at least extend the same privilege to the teacher.
The provincial governments are having quite a hard time at present to pay the cost of education, so I suggest that the dominion make a grant to each province in order that they can pay a cost of living bonus to the teachers. The teacher's position to-day, I believe hon. members will realize, is not any better than that of a great number of civil servants, and not as good as that of many common labourers in industry at the present time.
There is another group that I might mention. There are many people employed in the smaller stores. In the larger establishments I understand the help receive a cost of living bonus, but in the smaller stores, where only a few are employed, the cost of living bonus is not paid, or at least it is not compulsory. But if we look around we find that employees of all stores buy on practically the same market, so that if those employed by the large firms are entitled to the bonus, why not ' those in the smaller stores?
Then there is another group that I believe is also entitled to a cost of living bonus. This group comprises about one-third of the population of Canada. I refer now to the farmers. I am wondering whether some people believe that the farmers are entitled to a cost of living bonus. I remember when I came here first in 1936, we were told by someone who perhaps knew better, that the majority of farmers went to California or some other better climate in the winter, that each family had two or three cars, and a number of other such silly statements.
An hon. MEMBER; He must have been a Liberal.

speechtext:
The gentleman to whom I have reference did not sit very far from here at that time. He is not in the house now, and I hope he is happier than many of us here to-day are. Taking farmers and their families as a whole, I think the delegation that came here from Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba is a very fair sample of the average farmer of the west-and, I believe, the east as well. I think you will not find any of them lying around the streets drunk. I have not seen any. You do not find them wearing expensive clothes or doing anything that a respectable citizen of Canada should not do. Many compliments have been paid as to the calibre of these farmers and their wives. I believe they are entitled to great consideration at this time.
In the cities and towns we find that the man usually makes the living, while his wife looks after the home. That is so on some farms, but in many instances we find that the wife and children must get out and work so that the family may eat, pay their taxes and retain their home. Many of those farm homes are not as good as they should be; that is true in a large percentage of the cases. Some people on farms seem satisfied to do with less, and they are expected to do with less than people in the towns and cities. Why this should be so, I cannot understand, because, after all, farming is the basic industry of this country, and if you took away our farming, you would take away the lifeblood of the whole country.
Dealing with the question of wheat, we find that away back in 1935 the initial payment was 87| cents a bushel, basis No. 1 northern at Fort William, with participation certificates. That figure remained unchanged in 1936, with the restriction that the farmers could not use the wheat board unless the price of wheat fell below 90 cents a bushel. The same condition existed in 1937. In 1938, however, for some reason or another, the price was reduced to 80 cents a bushel. Perhaps the farmers were getting a little too prosperous; perhaps they were painting their homes, or something. Whatever the reason, the initial payment was reduced to 80 cents. In 1939 the first legislation brought in cut down the price to 60 cents a bushel; but after a great deal of controversy, with many speeches made in this house, over the radio and at meetings throughout the country, that was increased to 70 cents a bushel. At the same time there was introduced in this house the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which provided for a bonus if the crop was less than twelve bushels to the acre and the year was declared by the government to be an
The Address

Mr. Fair

emergency year. That policy was continued in 1940, but that year we had the additional payment of storage on wheat kept on the farm. In 1941 the same situation continued, except that the storage applied only to that undelivered portion of the quota which was held on the farm. In that year we also had regulations brought down under which farmers were encouraged to cut down their wheat acreage, and those doing so were given a bonus called the wheat acreage reduction bonus. I am not going into that to-night, but only a couple of months ago another bonus was announced. People call it by different names; I call it a general relief bonus, and I believe it was paid because the government felt so guilty. They must have felt guilty for a number of years past, but this year, because farm income was so low, they gave another general relief bonus to all farmers, grain growers, stock raisers or anything else.
This, it seems to me, is an open, frank admission by the government that their agricultural policy is not one on which Canada can live. I do not know of any body that should realize the plight of agriculture better than the government, and now they come along with another little hand-out to keep us dragging on a little longer. I would point out, however, that the latest bonus of 75 cents an acre, even with the other two bonuses to which I have referred, will not solve our wheat problem. There are two distinct problems. In the first place, the man who has no crop at all will not benefit in any way from a higher price for wheat. He will benefit through the payment of bonuses, provided they are high enough, but they are not high enough at the present time. On the other hand, a man who has a crop averaging more than twelve bushels to the acre does not benefit by any system of bonuses that may be put into effect. Therefore, to satisfy + lie man who has an average crop of twelve bushels or better, a higher price for wheat must be put into effect.
During past years several delegations have come to Ottawa trying to get something of benefit to the farming industry. It is realized by everyone in Canada that agricultural conditions are not satisfactory, and this applies to eastern as well as western Canada. I am not speaking of the west alone, as in the past some of us have been accused of doing. I believe the eastern farmers understand that their plight has been realized by the government also, since the government has agreed to pay the freight on feed grain coming from Fort William or points further west. So eastern farmers also are on the relief list. Let them not forget that; let them not think

we in the west are the only recipients of aid. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the wheat pools have come to Ottawa on various occasions, and each time I believe they were told that their demands were reasonable and would be given consideration by the government. But that consideration does not put any money into the pocket of the farmer. It does not pay his taxes; it does not buy shoes for the baby, or bread for the family. We must have a little more than consideration. During the time the government has been giving our problems consideration, our debts have been piling up, and no attempt has been made by the government to cut down interest rates on the money we owe in bank loans, mortgages and so forth.
We find also that the cost of machinery has continued to go up. This government held an investigation into that matter; the government of Saskatchewan also looked into it. On one occasion threats were made by the Minister of Agriculture, on behalf of the government, that if the machine companies did not bring down their prices, the government would take drastic action. The response of the machine companies was; one increase during the investigation, another immediately after it, and a number of others since that time, of which I have not kept track. Therefore the government does not mind at all if the farmers' costs go up.
Again, in some provinces, and particularly the province from which I come, attempts were made to ease the burdens of the farmers. But as soon as legislation was put on the statute books for this purpose, it was either done away with by the governor in council or referred to the courts, and there destroyed. If we look back to 1937 we remember that the President of the United States had to take certain action in connection with the supreme court of that country. He could not get his legislation into operation, and had to take action to make way for progressive legislation. I am not sure whether it may not be necessary to resort to action of that kind in this country in the near future.
Looking back over a period of sixty-four or sixty-five years, we find that the average price of wheat at Fort William was $1.17 a bushel, basis No. 1 northern. In the United States I understand the farmers at present are being paid $1.17. That is what they are guaranteed. We are guaranteed 70 cents. The Minister of Agriculture told us that the farmers could not expect to get rich during the first two years of this war. Now we are getting into the third year, and some of us think it is about time we started at least to make our expenses. During the third year

28S
The Address-Mr. Fair
of the first great war the average price of wheat was 82.06 a bushel, basis No. 1 northern at Fort William. As I have said, to-day we are guaranteed 70 cents, or approximately one-third the average price during the third year of the last war. We find that at that time, in the third year of the first great war, we could buy a binder for 8167. To-day the same binder costs 8347, or more than twice as much as it cost back in 1916. I believe this illustration will serve to show that the farmer has been caught both going and coming.
Conditions are not improving; they are gradually growing worse. At the present time there is a delegation in Ottawa seeking parity prices for agriculture, as well as other things. We wonder why we are not getting treatment similar to that received by other people in Canada. I believe most hon. members will recall that back in 1939 a limit of 5 per cent was placed on profits to be derived from government contracts. Because that was not sufficient for the industrialists, we find an order in council passed in the third week in August of 1939 which destroyed that legislation. To-day labour enjoys the same level of wages as obtained between 1926 and 1929. It has also an additional cost of living bonus. I am not objecting to that. In my opinion the workers are entitled to good pay. They work hard, and I do not object to the pay they receive. But I certainly must object when we as farmers are placed in a position where we have to produce at about half the cost of production. If industry is entitled to a removal of profit restrictions, if labour is entitled to the same wage level as existed between 1926 and 1929, with a cost of living bonus added, then I suggest that surely the farmer is entitled to the same level of prices as existed at that time.
The high price for wheat, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William between 1926 and 1929 was $1.61 a bushel. The average price in that same period was 81.35. Yet, although we have been told on different occasions that we are seeking equality of sacrifice in Canada, we are receiving a guaranteed price of only 70 cents a bushel. We find that in 1937-38 the average price for the year was 81.314 a bushel. Perhaps we would not mind so much if those low prices were necessary. But, looking over some of the literature I have, I am led to the conclusion that it is not necessary. I find this at page 14 of a booklet issued by the Searle Grain company:
It is interesting to note that one of the most eminent world authorities on the international wheat situation, Mr. Broomhall of London, said in an editorial in the Corn Trade News of August 27 as follows:
"Farmers in producing countries would have legitimate cause for . complaint if, in creating reserve supplies the price level were allowed to suffer by an artificial disparity between supply and demand."
With Mr. Broomhall's conclusion we most heartily concur, for we all know that the disparity which exists to-day between supply and demand has not been brought about by the free and open market, but is entirely the result of highly artificial conditions.
Again I ask: Why does the government allow that condition to exist? Again, by way of comparison: in 1928 the farmers of Canada received for their wheat crop 8441,000,000; and in 1941, even with the addition of the wheat acreage reduction bonus, the prairie farm assistance bonus and the general relief bonus, we receive approximately 8150,000,000
The delegation in Ottawa at the present time advocating, as I said before, a higher initial payment for wheat, and other matters along that line, are supported by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the western wheat pools and several other organizations. We find also that the northwest line elevtors' association has sent to the government, on at least two different occasions, briefs advocating an initial price or payment of 81.224 a bushel basis No. 1 northern, Fort William, and the Seaille Grain company advocates 81.20 a bushel.
Some people wonder whether we are entitled to that. I believe we are. As is known, at the present time the government is giving orders for the manufacture of certain war materials, and so forth. The people of Canada will have to pay for those things. They will have to pay the profits to industry, and the high wages now enjoyed by labour. We as farmers either directly or indirectly will pay a large percentage of those costs.
We find that on February 19, 1941, by order in council the government made an agreement with the grain companies whereby their handling and storage charges were guaranteed until the end of July, 1943. Was any such policy laid down or guaranteed to the farmers of Canada? No. In this connection I would add that this was asked for by the grain trade, but was not asked for by the wheat pools of western Canada. The pools were asked to come in on this, but refused to have anything to do with it. To-day the Saskatchewan pool is responsible for a large delegation which, I believe, the government should be ashamed to allow to come here to make its demands known, or try to do something about it.
We are producing food. I do not think there is any need for anybody to complain that that food will not be needed1. Prime
The Address-Mr. Fair

Minister Churchill has been quoted in the house on different occasions, and I intend to quote him again. On August 20, 1940, Mr. Winston Churchill said:
We shall do our best to encourage the building up of reserves of food all over the world so that there will always be held before the eyes of the people of Europe, including the Germans, the certainty that the shattering of nazi power would bring to them all immediate food, freedom and peace.
And the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on October 18, 1941, said: "Wheat held in reserve constitutes an invaluable war asset." The farmers of Canada are willing to produce. They complain at home, through their members and now by delegation. But we have not found them going on a sit-down strike. They continue to produce, anyway, and they are doing everything possible in the war, even to the extent of sending their last son over there to fight. I know that is true in dozens of instances. Why are we treated in this way? I believe that since the delegation came to Ottawa, it has been successful in meeting the government. I hold in my hand a clipping in point. It appeared in yesterday's Ottawa Journal, and states, in part: ''Renewed, helpful and I believe fruitful consideration" will be given the representations of prairie wheat farmers, Prime Minister Mackenzie King to-day promised four hundred farmer-delegates who came to Ottawa. . . .
And so on. Let us hope that this consideration will be far more fruitful than some of the other things the Prime Minister has attempted in earlier days. We hope that will happen. Then, later in the article:
Finance Minister Ilsley-he was one of those who heard the farmers' submissions-had to meet financial requirements and consider petitions like that of the wheat growers, with relation to the broad financial needs of a dominion at war, Mr. King added.
The Prime Minister, speaking in confidential manner to the men of the west, said the government had not given any closer attention to any question than agriculture. He felt that Canadian farmers would agree no branch of agricul-ure had experienced more difficulty than the wheat-growing branch represented by Saskatchewan.
We are to get fruitful consideration.

speechtext: Yes, and that the fruit does not disappear before it reaches the farmer. Both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) agreed' that the requests were fair-

speechtext:
-and reasonable. It is up to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to find the money. During the past two and a half years the Minister of Finance has been finding a lot of money, much of which has gone for purposes of destruction. We are also told that we shall be called on for far greater sums. If the Minister of Finance can find money to pay cost-plus to industry and to pay wages, through industry, to labour, he should also make it his business to pay at least the cost of production plus a small profit to the farmers. If the minister has not learned enough about money to know how to do that, I would suggest that we forgo the services of our member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) for a little while so that he may advise the minister how and where he can get this money. The minister, no doubt, has a fountain pen, and he will find out that it will work just as well for the Bank of Canada, to create credit, as it does for the chartered banks.
In the Western Producer of January 29, 1942, there are one or two items in a letter in the open forum, which I should like to read. Here is the first one:
About 1912 the Grain Growers' Association sent a delegation of 400 men to Ottawa to lay our demands before the government of that day. After we had dropped all our bombs, Wilfrid Laurier only talked to them for three minutes and in other words told them to go home and the government would run its own business. In 1920 our demand for a wheat board became so urgent that we built a new political party known as Progressives. Every candidate was pledged to support a wheat board policy when he took his seat in the house at Ottawa. We swept this province (Saskatchewan) clean save for one Liberal (Mr. Motherwell). During the last week of the campaign he figured his seat was slipping so the paper with the people's viewpoint, the Leader Post, came out with a front page advertisement: Vote for Motherwell and return of the wheat board. When he got to Ottawa Mackenzie King made him minister of agriculture and he proved to be an enemy to a wheat board. The Progressive party landed in Ottawa after the 1921 election with 64 members, mostly all from the west.
The Liberal high command had seen this storm brewing in the west, so Tom Crerar was sent out in the guise of a believer in this new movement. He led his army right into the battlefield at Ottawa and then deserted us. In the terms of to-day he would be known as a fifth columnist and was just twenty years ahead of King Leopold of Belgium, who also turned his army over to the enemy.
I believe there is one way in which the farmers can get something better than they are getting at the present time. They have been promised consideration for a number of years, but their plight is becoming worse the farther we go along. My suggestion to the

The Address-Mr. McLean
farmers is to organize. During the last election some were quite satisfied to vote for 70-cent wheat, but to-day the farmers of the west are coming here with a petition in the one hand and a hat in the other pleading:
' Won't you give us something better?" As soon as they send true representatives here, they will probably get some place. We are not satisfied to-day with 70 cents a bushel for wheat, either on the farm or at Fort William. For some years past the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) has had a resolution on the order paper asking for 95 cents a bushel, basis one northern, at the local elevator, and he has now a resolution on the order paper reading as follows:
Whereas the prices of farm machinery, all costs of living and farm wages have increased due to the war:
Therefore be it resolved that in the opinion of this house parliament should immediately take such steps as are necessary to ensure the farmers of Canada a fixed price of not less than one dollar ($1) per bushel for number 1 northern wheat at their local elevator for a farmer's delivery quota, as defined by the Canadian Wheat Board.
And to take care of the man who does not have a crop, I have the following resolution on the order paper:
That in the opinion of this house the government should introduce such amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act that it will become a sound crop insurance scheme.
In conclusion, might I suggest that the first duty of any government is to look after the welfare and happiness of its people? In this I believe this government has failed miserably. Since this government came into office in 1935, there have been great numbers of men and women who could not get work, and there are still thousands to-day who cannot get a job. The farmers have been allowed to work, but we cannot get the cost of production. So what is the use of working, some people say. The government has failed to prevent production costs from going up. In view of the fact that farmers directly or indirectly pay most of our Canadian taxes, I think something should be done on their behalf, and done right away.
I believe the government should also take better care of the soldiers of the last war and their dependents, as well as the soldiers of this war and their dependents. I believe a completely new deal should be given the soldiers of the last war who are still labouring under the policies of the Soldier Settlement Board. I shall deal with this later.
There are several other matters I should like to mention, but I have not the time to-night. I would, however, ask that the organized farmers' representatives be given a
place on all boards having to do with farmers' problems, and when I say "organized farmers", I do not mean that any political party friend, whether or not he is a success on his own, should be given a place on these boards.
Parity prices for wheat and all other farm products should be guaranteed, and there should be an amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to provide a sound crop insurance scheme, which is badly needed. In addition, I believe that the Winnipeg grain exchange should be closed because it is a gambling den that has no place in Canada to-day.
All these things and more can be done by making proper use of our financial system, whereby credit and currency will be issued in terms of public need, as advocated by the Prime Minister prior to the 1935 election when he said:
A national central bank is necessary in order that currency and credit may be made available in terms of public need to meet the domestic and industrial requirements of the Canadian people.
If ever that time has arrived, it is now. The farmers of Canada are not asking for charity and do not want it. All we want is treatment equal to that given to other Canadians, and we must be granted that treatment; We cannot have Canadian unity, so often pleaded for by the Prime Minister and others in this house, as long as one section of the population feasts while another goes hungry. Hitler of Germany must be licked at all costs. But we have Hitlers in Canada who must also be licked if the Canadian people are to enjoy to the fullest the liberties to which we are entitled and the abundance at our disposal.

Mr. Speaker, the debate on the motion before the house has now continued for about eight days. But, as I am sure hon. members will agree that nobody has shown less inclination than I have to prolong debate or to indulge in* tiresome and vain repetition, I am impelled on this occasion to crave your indulgence, sir, and that of the house while I try to give expression to a few thoughts.
The first words I would utter would be words of tribute to our fellow citizens who at our call and on our behalf have undertaken the heavy, heavy task of combat-the men of the army, the navy, the merchant marine, the air force, and the women of the nursing services. This is not the place, I know, where hon. members are wont to give expression to their deepest feelings, and I am not going to indulge in heroics, but I do think it is due to these valiant men and women that from our plac*
The Address-Mr. McLean

as members of the parliament of their country we tell them, not once, or twice, that we remember them; that we recognize that the task laid on them is different, very different in kind from that of all others. I believe that the words which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) used in this house on May 20, 1940, could well be repeated time and again. He said, as reported at page 49 of Hansard of that year:
Everything that we can do, every help that we can give, every contribution that we can make, every comfort, great or small, that we must surrender is as a grain of sand compared with the treasure which they offer on the altar of humanity.
Or the words of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), spoken when he was Minister of Finance. I do not remember whether it was when he was delivering the budget speech or the speech on the war appropriation bill, but on some such occasion he gave expression to words which I have never forgotten, and which I think should be heard and remembered throughout the war by every citizen of Canada. I am not sure that I can recall the exact words, but they were to this effect, "I shall not disgrace the word 'sacrifice' by applying it to anything save the gift of life itself."
