I wish, Mr. Speaker, that it were possible for the response to those words from every corner of the house to be heard by every member of our armed forces, wherever he or she may be found. I wish it were possible that they could penetrate to those who are languishing in prison camps and in hospitals far across the sea. For those who have passed forever beyond the reach of all human expression, we can only offer tribute to their memory, and to the homes from which they have gone, sympathy, for which I shall not try to find words.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, that the question of the method of enlistment for service in our armed forces overseas should have become a contentious one. I believe that this question has been magnified out of all proportion to its importance. There is no use, however, in indulging in vain regrets over what we would like to have had; we must take the facts as they are. . I am bound to recognize that, in the words of the speech from the throne, our war effort is being impaired by controversy raging over what has now become a contentious question. Up to date I have refrained from discussing this question either in Ottawa or in my own riding. I have felt that no

good could come from my stirring up questions on which people were likely to have sharp differenees of opinion. During my election campaign I intentionally and resolutely kept it from being made an issue in my riding, largely for the sake of the character of the riding. I thought it would have been unfair, perhaps unfair to my opponent, if I had tried to make that an issue in my riding. But I must confess that, in common with nearly all members of both Liberal and Conservative parties, I am bound by the speeches which were made by the leaders of both these two parties prior to the last election. It is under these circumstances that I wish to take a few minutes to make my position clear to the members of the house and to my constituents.
I want to say a word first about the compulsory selective service in connection with civilian occupations. I am only going to touch on it, because I do not think there is very much difference of opinion, certainly on the principle. As the Prime Minister pointed out, authority for this was given by the National Resources Mobilization Act. The only question is how soon, in what manner, and to what extent that ought to be put into effect. Personally, I think that prompt action should be taken. In my section, as in many others, the farmers are having a very difficult time. I find men enlisting from some of our factories whom I think it would have been better to keep in the factories. On the other hand, I even know of toolmakers-mechanics who are perhaps scarcest of all-who during the depression went out to operate little farms and are still on those farms. As I say, I am not going to dwell on this question, but I shall await with great interest the statement which I expect we shall hear from the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) as to the plan he has in mind. I would suggest this, however, that the temporary postponement in connection with farm help is not sufficient and not satisfactory. A farmer must be able to plan his work somewhat ahead. There are some farms where population is fairly large though they are not very good farms and not producing very much. On the other hand, there are very good large farms where production is very high; the farm is well operated, but help very, very scarce. The same treatment should not be given in both those cases; and I do not think it is possible for a man in the office of the district registrar to deal with these; I think there ought to be somebody closer to the farmer, closer to the community, in a better position to judge of the circumstances surrounding each case. As I have said, however, nearly everything I have

The Address-Mr. McLean
to say on this question is merely repetition, and I do not want to weary the house by repeating what has already been said better than I can say it.
Coming to the question of compulsory service for the armed forces overseas, I always have believed and I still believe that the voluntary system is best. I have listened with great attention to the arguments of those who take a different view. I respect their opinion, and I do not for one moment question their sincerity, but, for reasons which I shall give, I still retain my preference for the voluntary system.
Having said this, however, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that the preservation of our country and our empire, freedom, everything which is now in imminent peril, must be placed before any and all other considerations; and if and when, in my judgment, based on facts which become apparent to me or on information that I receive from those I consider best able to judge, whether inside or outside the cabinet, I consider the time has come when we can more effectively prosecute the war by compulsory enlistment for overseas in our combatant forces, I shall not hesitate to change my position and shall support it. Because I want to be free to take that changed position if and when circumstances warrant it, I am in favour of a plebiscite by which the people will free me and the government from the solemn pledge given under very different circumstances.
I am in favour of the voluntary system because of the effectiveness of the army itself. After all, victory is what we want-victory in a fight. All considerations of what is fair or logical must be subordinated to that-victory in a fight.
Our army must be trained, it must be well equipped, it must be given arms and munitions, and all that. But after you have trained it, supplied it with equipment, and given it proper leadership, it still has to fight; and it seems to me that in our discussion far too little consideration has been given to the fact that the men have to face the terror, the horror, the bloodshed and the violence of battle. They must face dismemberment and even death, and still go on and fight and fight and win victory. That takes something that is simply not in the coward; it takes something that is simply not in the slacker; it takes something that is simply not in the sort of man of whom I have heard some member speak, the man who says, "I am willing to go, but I am going to wait until the government tells me." It is not in the type of man or the man who hangs around for a year or more trying to get a commission or some other preferment.
I speak from experience as a private soldier in a Canadian infantry battalion, and as a platoon commander and company commander in a British regiment, commanding both volunteers and forced recruits; and I say that when a unit finds itself in a desperate position, its members do not want to feel that, scattered among them or supporting them on their flanks, are men who have had to be forced to fight. They want to feel that they are supported by men who are imbued with the same spirit as themselves, men who will come promptly, quickly and voluntarily when their countiy calls them.
When men tell me that because I am in favour of the voluntary system as against the compulsory I am not true, not loyal to the men who are at the front, I sometimes wonder whether these people have any conception of the sort of job we have given these men to do. We admit that as far as the air force and the navy are concerned, and especially the air force, we shall not have compulsion. Why? Well, I suppose it is because it is thought that men in the air force should be of the very highest type of valour and daring. Will any man tell me, however, that of the humblest private soldier who carries a rifle and bayonet into battle there is not going to be demanded the utmost in the way of human valour and endurance? And those qualities are required in a much higher degree in this war in which men are acting very much on their own-much more so than in the last war when to a large extent men fought in large masses.
I have heard it said by some members of the house that the voluntary system has been a failure. I do not admit it. I cannot give exact figures to date, but I believe that between 400,000 and 430,000 men have volunteered in the various armed forces for service in any part of the world. I believe that during last year somewhere between 150,000 and 180,000 men similarly volunteered. These were accepted in both cases, after those were rejected who were unfit physically or otherwise. I have not the total figures for my own riding, but I have approximate figures for my own home town, of between nine and ten thousand. In that town almost if not quite 800 men have voluntarily enlisted and been accepted for active service in the various branches of the armed forces. Of these, 200 at least are now overseas and about 200 in the air force.
But, Mr. Speaker, if enlistment has not been all that some might have expected, I do not put the blame for this on the young men of the country. I do not, I cannot, and I never will believe that our men are so lacking in

The Address-Mr. McLean

patriotism that they will not respond when their native land and the native land of their fathers is in peril, if that call is made clearly and in a proper manner to them.
A number of factors have militated against enlistment. In the first place, in some districts there was quite a long delay before the local non-permanent active militia units were mobilized. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that a different system was adopted in this war from that which was followed in the last war-and a much better one. In the last war units were mobilized without identification except for a number, and men were enlisted in them from all over the province. In this war the late Minister of National Defence, Mr. Rogers, instituted the system of retaining the identity of the non-permanent active militia units in the establishments of the active force in order to preserve the county spirit, the town spirit, the regimental spirit in the active overseas units. That was a good idea. But the necessary result was, of course, that in some districts men waited sometimes months and more than a year before their unit was mobilized. They waited with a good deal of impatience, and many men lost a good deal of the zeal and fervour with which they were imbued when the call to arms first came.
I remember very well the situation in the counties of Grey and Simcoe. The Grey-Simcoe Foresters were mobilized finally as a unit of the 4th division. These men pleaded with members to ask the Minister of National Defence that they be mobilized. They begged for months and months to have this done. The same thing happened in connection with many other units, and this was one of the factors that did have an effect on enlistment.
Another feature was the opinion, pretty commonly held before and for some time after the war, that because of a change in the nature of warfare it was very unlikely that there would be any occasion to send a large expeditionary force overseas-not as a matter of policy at all, but as a matter of war strategy, or whatever the proper military term is. There was also the idea that Canada was to be the arsenal of the empire, and that idea naturally turned men's minds to the duty they owed the country to remain in the occupations in which they found themselves, agricultural or industrial.
I have heard the suggestion that the government itself did not give that clarion call for enlistment to arms which it might have given. I am not going to enter upon any debate on that point, but I do say that the Minister of National Defence, the Prime Minister, and others, did make very strong appeals

which I thought did not receive the attention and the publicity in headlines in various sections of the press which they might have been given. .
Be that as it may, however, there were other voices in influential positions which did not speak in the accents that we heard in 1914. Let me give an example. The president of one of our large universities was reported, shortly after the war broke out, to have advised his students not to be in a hurry to enlist, but to finish their courses. I am not saying he was wrong, but I cannot help contrasting that with the attitude adopted by the president of the great university of Toronto in the autumn of 1914. I well recall how Sir Robert, then Doctor Falconer, called his students together in the autumn of 1914. He did not speak to them of the value to themselves or the country of their academic career or the places they were going to fill in civilian life. He put the issue clearly before them; he told them that they, of all classes, owed more to the country and to the way of life that was threatened, and he pointed out very clearly and forcefully that to them first of all the call to arms came. And how they responded! The voice was different from that of 1939. They enlisted in very large numbers. There was no waiting for commissions; there was none of that. Scores of them never came back, and of those who did very many never realized aspirations of their student days. There are hon. members of this house who were members of the classes of 1914, 1915, 1916, and I am sure there is nothing of which they are more proud than the lead given by their president in those days and the way in which those men responded to it.
Another feature is the popularity of two branches of the armed service-the navy and the air force. Someone may say that this is not an important matter, but I think it is. Men in the navy and the air force have been in action much sooner than those in the army, and naturally ardent youth is more anxious to get into the branches which are in action first. I suppose there is something more spectacular about those two branches. If all those who have been waiting to enlist in the air force and the navy should be added to those who have enlisted in the army, the figures would look very much better.
While speaking of that, I want to compliment the Minister of National Defence very highly upon what I understand is a proposal to give a dress uniform to the men of the army. I sincerely trust no single voice will be raised against that on account of the expense. The battle-dress no doubt is a

The Address-Mr. McLean
splendid dress for battle, but it must be admitted that it is not a dressy uniform; it looks rather slouchy and does not do justice to the men when they are on the streets of our towns and villages. It is not fair that when men of the air force or of the navy come home for a week-end and go out to some social function, they have smart, neatlooking uniforms of which they are proud, while the poor chap in the army has to wear this slouchy-looking battle-dress. When men come out of our factories and off the farms or out of the mines and attend some social function, they can take off their working clothes and put on a collar and tie and a neat suit; and if civilians can afford to dress up in that way, I hope there will be no voice raised against the expense of giving to these men who are going to fight our battles a dress of which they may be proud and which will encourage them to hold their heads higher when they are off duty.
There is another factor which has had a great deal of influence on recruiting. Ever since the first voice was raised in this house- on the eve of a recruiting campaign, as it was-calling for conscription; and as that voice was taken up by the press, by public speakers and, in gome instances I am told, even by military officers assigned to the duty of recruiting, the chilly, deadening effect of that cry was felt on recruiting from coast to coast. It was felt in every meeting called for the purpose of organizing recruiting campaigns. I am sure every hon. member who has had anything to do with trying to assist in recruiting knows the truth of that statement.
It was my privilege some two or three months ago to attend a dinner meeting. The auspices were very favourable. We were in a comfortable room, had a splendid guest speaker; there was a large and expectant audience. The speaker had recently returned from England, and he gave one of the most magnificent addresses to which I have ever listened. He told of the valour of the people of Britain, the suffering of the men, women and children, the magnificent organization of all resources; all these things were pictured in words that held that audience thrilled. I was sitting near the back of the room looking over that audience, and among them were quite a number of men of military age who were not in uniform-business men, professional men. As that speaker told of the marvellous fight that the people of Britain were putting up for us, I fancy that some of those young men felt a little uncomfortable; I fancy they were beginning to give pretty serious consideration to where their duty lay. The speaker ended that wonderful address with
44561-19$
a strong appeal. What was the appeal? Was it an appeal to those men to get into uniform? Not at all. He ended with a strong statement that the responsibility of deciding who should go into the army should be laid on the government of the country. I fancy those young men settled back into their comfortable chairs a little more comfortably when the responsibility was taken from their own conscience and placed on some other body What, in effect, are all these voices saying? To the young man to whom the call of his country, the voice of duty, is strong and insistent, the voice which he is about to obey, they are saying, "That stern voice of duty with which you have been wrestling for the last few days or weeks is not the voice to which you should listen. Wait; wait; we are going to create another voice. We are going to put a man-made law on the statute books of your country, and that is the voice to which you are to listen. Never mind about that voice which calls you, that powerful impulse in the life of every young man; never mind that; that is not the voice. Let us have another authority; wait until that man-made law is put upon the statute books of your country."
I am not sitting in judgment on any other man; I respect the opinion of every other man, and I would be the last to impute any improper motives. I know that many of my friends who want conscription are actuated, as I am, by the very highest and best patriotic motives. But I say that during the last year, in so far as the voices of which I have been speaking have had the effect I indicate, they have sinned against the spirit of a whole generation.
I recall some twenty-six years ago, Mr. Speaker, getting into conversation with an old shepherd up in the highlands of Scotland, where I had gone to spend ten days leave and to look up some relatives. During the course of our conversation the question of compulsory service came up, since that legislation had been enacted only recently. The old shepherd said to me, "As far as yon village is concerned, and all up the glen, we are not subject to the draft." I was puzzled for a moment, until I realized what I ought to have known, that in this particular region, where men had always sprung to arms at the first call, whether of king or of clan, long before compulsory service had been considered every able-bodied man had joined the colours. No wonder the blood in German veins often ran chill when they learned that across from them was the famous 51st Highland division! That is the class of man we need in our armed forces if we are to achieve victory.
The Address-Mr. McLean

As I have said, if and when I am convinced that we must have compulsory service, I will support it; but I know that in my riding, as in many ridings, there are families that will not be subject to the draft; and it is my hope that in my riding, as in many ridings throughout the country, there may be whole communities whose men already will have answered the higher call of duty, without waiting for the draft. I believe with all my heart that in peace or war the motive behind all heroic or unselfish action is not the compulsion of man-made law but the more compelling force of noble impulses, which are the natural gift of youth; and I have not lost faith, as I will never lose faith, that the young men of our country, when the call is put to them clearly and properly, will respond in sufficient numbers to fill up every establishment that may be decided upon by the Department of National Defence in order to carry on the war. I must say, however, that I do object most strenuously to making synonymous total war and compulsory training for overseas service. These are made synonymous by many public speakers and in the press. I am not in favour of compulsory service for overseas, yet I take second place to no man in my desire that Canada should prosecute the war to the very fullest extent possible.
In the short time left to me, I want to deal with a matter that is rather distasteful. I have tried to make my position clear to the house and to the people of my riding. I have not been driven to do so by the gibes or threats of any newspaper; nor have I refrained from doing so until now because of the motives which have been attributed to me, and to all other Liberal members from Ontario, by a Toronto newspaper. I heard the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) give the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), I think it was, some good advice on one occasion. He said no one should ever get into an argument with a newspaper, who does not own one. Well, I do not own a newspaper, and I am not going to get into an argument with one. As a matter of fact, I have every reason to possess a high regard for the press. In my riding we are fortunate in having a very high-class weekly press. One weekly newspaper is edited by a life-long Conservative, a good friend of mine, who nearly always opposes me in politics, but I want to say that the news items in that newspaper are always absolutely reliable. That man would no more think of selling coloured news to his readers than an honest merchant would think of selling contaminated food to his customers; and the editorials appearing

in that newspaper, though they usually disagree with the leader and members of the party to which I belong, are always fair argument.
I would that the same standard of journalism characterized some of the daily newspapers which serve our section of the country. For some time past the Toronto Globe and Mail has contained offensive references to Liberal members, culminating on December 12, 1941, in this article:
There are 82 Ontario seats in the dominion House of Commons. Fifty-seven of these are occupied by Liberals. Not one of these Liberals has yet risen to lay before the house the clearly revealed opinion of his constituents on this all important question of compulsory selective service. This is a shocking state of affairs. We all know very well that Mr. King is cooking up some emasculated form of mobilization ingeniously contrived to appease, palliate and placate some without offending others. We all know that, true to his long established technique of enforcing party discipline, he is holding over the members' heads a number of unfulfilled appointments which each of his followers thinks he has a chance of filling. There are vacancies in the Senate; there is a rumoured shuffling of the cabinet, there are committees needing paid chairmen, and commissions whose members have not yet been named. The carrot is being held before the nose of the donkey as an inducement to that greedy and fatuous animal to walk soberly in the straight and narrow path of political opportunism.
I might indulge in an angry, recriminatory attack on that newspaper, but I am not going to do so. I am too much in earnest to adopt any such course; but I do say that every hon. member possessed of a spark of self respect; every hon. member who prizes the good opinion of his friends and his countrymen as to the integrity of his intentions, public as well as private; every hon. member who has a proper conception of the duty he owes to maintain the reputation as well as the character of the institution in which his people have honoured him with membership, every such member has not only the right but the duty to make an indignant protest against such an editorial. I heartily agree with the desirability of preserving political independence, and hon. members know full well that there have been ample evidences of it in this house. Members of both the Conservative and Liberal parties have repeatedly voted against their parties without being disciplined for so doing. Every hon. member knows, as our constituents may not know, that the popular characterization of a party whip is simply grotesque. I need not repeat the duties of the whip; hon. members know them. One of the duties of a party whip is to assist Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the other whips, in the orderly arrangement of debates in the house. He has minor duties

The Address-Mr. McLean
to perform, such as seating and office arrangements, and he also performs the very important duty of acting as liaison between private members and the cabinet. He keeps the cabinet informed as to the views of hon. members on various questions, something which cannot always1 be done between caucuses, and cannot always be done even at caucuses, when the membership is very large. I hold that the popular characterization of a party whip is simply grotesque, and it is unfortunate that once in a while even hon. members in the house, quite innocently I think, will slip into the jargon of the street and talk about the crack of the party whip, thus giving force to the opinion popularly held.
One word more about party independence. Political independence is an important, a precious thing. But let me say to people outside the house, and to the newspaper in question, something which hon. members know quite well, that political independence, like all precious coins, has its counterfeit. Sometimes it is difficult for the public to distinguish between the genuine and the fake. There are times when it takes a good deal more courage on the part of a member to vote for his party than to rise in his place and vote against it. Every hon. member knows that.
There may be, and there are times when the position of a party is sound and wise; but considerations of passing popular public opinion, considerations of the safety of a member in his own riding at the next election, and consideration of the desirability of laudation of headlines in the newspapers-all these things make it a great deal easier, and indeed offer quite a temptation to vote against one's party. There you have the false, the fraud; there you have the counterfeit.
And, Mr. Speaker, to get back to the metaphorical donkey and carrot, let me point out that there is more than one kind of carrot which is supposed to make the teeth of the donkey water. I am not so sure that the editor of the paper in question, or the news editor or the gentleman who arranges the headlines, has not a few carrots stuck away in his pocket which he thinks are very, very sweet to the palate of certain politicians. He does not just hold them before the nose of the animal; he feeds them to him. And he does not feed them in half-pint measures, either; he feeds them in bushel basketfuls. In fact, I think sometimes he feeds them in such large doses that the effect must be somewhat nauseating to the creature to whom it is fed.
My time is almost up, but before resuming my seat I should like to refer to one other
editorial in this paper. I shall not take time to read it all; the general public has read the editorial to which the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) referred last night. Speaking about the speech of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) in the house, the editorial states:
And he was rewarded for his effort by some of the most disgraceful evidence of petty political spleen that the house has ever witnessed. After such an episode it is hard to have much respect for parliament.
Lest I might seem to be prejudiced, I should like to say that I have the very highest regard; indeed I have reason to have the very highest regard for the hon. member for Parkdale. I want to pay this tribute to him. I was a little annoyed when, in his first speech he suggested a change in leadership; but I have not formed my opinion of him because of the speeches he has made in the house. I have formed my opinion from the work he did in a committee on which I served. I know the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) and the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macmillan), who was chairman of the committee, will agree with me when I say that although the committee was one in connection with the activities of which this member might have been expected to have had a great deal to say, the attitude of the hon. member for Parkdale was most modest and helpful. No member on the committee did more to assist in having its work carried on successfully and free from party bias than did the hon. member for Parkdale. That is my opinion of the hon. member who made the speech to which reference is made in the newspaper editorial. I pay him that tribute, because I do not want anyone to think that when I take objection to the editorial, I have any feeling against him.

speechtext:
The man who wrote this editorial knew perfectly well that the actions of the Prime Minister and other Liberal members in the house did not constitute an insult to parliament. I was not in the house when that speech was delivered'- and no one has a higher regard than I have for the hon. member. As a matter of fact, verv
The Address-Mr. McLean

often when he is about to deliver a speech, in order that 1 may hear him better I go to the other side of the chamber and stand behind the curtains, so that I may be in front of him when he is speaking.
Since the last election in my constituency there have been practically no Liberals or Conservatives, as such. The people there work together. They do Red Cross work, act on committees for the sale of bonds and war savings certificates, and on committees for recruiting-Liberals and Conservatives together. None work harder on those committees than some who at election times oppose me. I would hang my head in abject shame if I were to go back to that riding knowing that the people believed that the conduct of this house and the motives actuating the member's were such as depicted in the Globe and Mail of Toronto.
We may be a mediocre lot. God help us, I know we are. When I am no longer a candidate for my constituency I hope the Liberal party in that constituency will be able to persuade the very best, most honest, capable and respected Liberal in the riding to accept the nomination. At the next election I hope the Conservative party will be able to choose as our opponent the most capable, honest and upright among their group in the constituency of Simcoe East. I should like that no matter who is elected, the people in that constituency will have confidence that they are well represented in the House of Commons. But, Mr. Speaker, we are not going to be able to persuade such men to run for office; they will not do it, if they believe that the conduct of the House of Commons and the motives w'hich actuate members are such as have been depicted week after week, week after week by the Globe and Mail. No, you will not be able to get such men to enter politics.
I endeavour not to be angry, but I do plead with that paper: Write as strong editorials as you like, either in favour of or against any policy; condemn the action of any man you think is -wrong; but, in the name of democracy, w'hich has been falling in country after country, country after country, and which is falling into disregard even in our own country, do not continue to aid and abet those who hold democracy in contempt and who unintentionally, if not intentionally, are doing their utmost to banish democracy from our country.
I should like in closing to quote one paragraph w'ritten by a man whom I am proud to call a fellow townsman. I refer to Doctor Stephen Leacock, late of McGill university who, in the Canadian Spokesman of January, 1941, wrote an article which I commend to all hon. members. I commend it

particularly to his very dear friends and admirers in my own riding which has been his home all his life, although he has journeyed down to McGill university every winter to give his students there the benefit of his wisdom. He is speaking of "The whole duty of a citizen," and says:
With all this in mind the word at the moment is "my country right or wrong." It may be a poor maxim in peace time but in war time there's nothing like it. Turn yourself into a pig-headed patriot and support all those in authority w'ithout criticism or quibble. If our Prime Minister and cabinet are not the biggest men in Canada, I'm going to think so till the end of the war anyway. After that I can turn back into a Conservative and look for some fun again.
He ends up with these words:
There it stands. To submit and to obey: To pay gladly: To applaud the brave: To honour the fallen, to aid and comfort those bereft. In that lies a united nation. You and I can at least be a humble part of it.

Mr. Speaker, I should like first to congratulate the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. McLean) who has just taken his seat. I am not sure, but I believe it was his maiden speech in this house; and while I disagreed with almost every part of it, I should like to congratulate him on the excellence of his presentation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me make myself clear. I oppose this plebiscite with every power at my command. Bad as is government by order in council; bad as is government by a vast majority; bad as is a government by statements to the press and over the radio, nothing can compare in infamy with the dodging of responsibility by the method of the plebiscite. After hearing and reading the impassioned speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) against Prussianism and dictatorships, it is indeed a revelation to find that same Prime Minister going to the dictators for his inspiration, because, while the plebiscite is not and never has been a recognized institution in the realm of democracy and parliamentary government, it has been a most effective weapon wielded upon frequent occasions by the dictators in the past ten years, and an instrument which usually the dictators have been able to use to their own advantage. "Eine, Volk, Eine Land, Eine Reich, Eine Fuehrer-Vote Ja -Heil Hitler!"-have been the methods Hitler used to settle matters in Germany.
The time has long passed when compulsory selective service for any part of the world has been of paramount necessity. This parliament should have enacted the necessary legislation after Dunkirk and the fall of France. The

The Address-Mr. Adamson
need now is even more imperative than ever. It is possible that it may already be too late. I believe that the declaration of war on Germany should have been preceded by a selective service act. Had this been done, all the trouble, all the bitterness, yes and all the violence that we may yet see would have been avoided. If there is one thing the last war has taught us it is that there can be no half measures in waging war. This war has also shown us that half measures mean defeat, degradation, humiliation and the infestation of our country by the enemy. Let it not be said of us in this House of Commons that we were incapable of seeing and doing our duty.
There is at present before this house a bill advocating a distinctive national flag for Canada. If we lose this war, we shall have a new flag, but it will contain the swastika or the rising sun of Japan. If this war is won for us, and the other united nations consider that we have not done our full part, they may themselves decide on alterations in the flag of Canada, and the alteration may contain the stars and stripes or some other emblem. Let us be worthy of the flag we have before talking about getting a new one.
While considering Canadian nationalism and basking in the Statute of Westminster, it might be interesting to see what other nations think of us. We have heard much talk about Canadian-United States unity. Let us see what is happening in the United States this month, February, 1942. On February 16 a large number, several millions of men, are required to report to the United States authorities for service with the United States armed forces anywhere in the world. My United States friends tell me that there are over 400,000 Canadians registered in the United States, and they estimate that over
100,000	more .have failed for various reasons to register. A high percentage of Canadian citizens in the United States are single men of military age, and it has been estimated that between 30,000 and 40,000 Canadian citizens will find themselves in one or other of the vulnerable categories, and that half of them will be in category A 1. I am informed by United States friends that this means single men who would be in our medical category A, men who are not employed on work of national importance. Probably some 15,000 to 20,000 Canadians will find themselves called on February 16 to join the armed forces of the country which gives them protection, namely, the United States of America. What a fine position for a great sovereign nation like Canada to be in! We are unwilling to call up our own nationals inside Canada, but our realist neighbours the Americans have no hesitation in calling up
our nationals resident in their country. In this war the United States is not a safe place to be.
The normal procedure under international law is to give allied nationals the option of serving with their own forces, if they can join up with them. However, the terms of service must be similar. The Canadian army is better paid than the United States army, and dependents' allowances and other advantages are granted in the Canadian armed forces. A number of Canadians caught in the United States draft might therefore elect to serve in the Canadian armed forces. Unless, however, we have conscription for overseas service, the terms of service in the United States army are much more onerous than in the Canadian army under the National Resources Mobilization Act.	Our good
friends the Americans know this and, I feel sure, will not look with favour on Canadians called for service in the United States anywhere in the world who elect to join the Canadian army for service in Canada only. As one Washington reporter put it to me, "We are not going to let your men shirk their responsibilities and return to Canada and become home defence units."	He called
them "campfire cuddlers." Is it a great thing to be a Canadian; or is it?
I now come to the reasons why I so strongly advocate the course I do.
The recent announcement as to the Canadian army to be formed overseas is of great interest. It, however, cannot come as much of a surprise to anyone who has given any thought to the problem, nor can it, in the light of the situation in the Pacific, be considered excessive. Indeed, in comparison with the efforts put forward by our sister dominions of Australia and New Zealand, it is very meagre.
I am pleased to see, however, that the government has followed very closely the formations I recommended in a speech made in this house on May 8 last, as reported at page 2687 of Hansard. I suggested, in the light of the battle of Greece, that we needed:
.	. . four infantry divisions, and with each
division a complete armoured brigade and complete artillery units. Besides that, I suggest that we need two complete armoured divisions. We must be able to maintain in Canada in training complete reinforcements for these formations, assuming an annual wastage of one-third. That I submit is, in the light of recent events, the minimum commitment that we can be called upon to complete.
That was last May. I went on to discuss what this would mean in man-power, and I estimated an active army overseas of 200,000 men. Add to these the air force and the navy, 100,000, and you will have an overseas force
The Address-Mr. Adamson

of approximately 300,000. With the exception that I suggested an armoured brigade with each infantry division, and the proposal now is for two armoured brigades with the infantry army corps of three infantry divisions, my proposals in May, 1941, and the government's proposal of January, 1942, are identical, the tragic difference being that the government waited nine months to give birth to its plan, a plan which must now be considered to impose but a light burden indeed on our man-power, because it will require enlistments of but between six and seven thousand a month for the army.
The present situation, which has mobilized every able-bodied man, woman and child in Australia, calls for equally drastic action from Canada. A force such as the Canadian army, small as it is in comparison with those of the other belligerents of the united powers, will call for an even greater force on the home front and in the munitions factories. It is because of the necessity of maintaining a proper balance between the fighter in the field and the fighter in the factory that I so strongly recommend compulsory selective service.
From the military angle, in the middle of October, 1941, we were unable to supply even the small number of men needed to provide first reinforcements for two battalions sent to Hong Kong without including 138 men who had not received their full advanced training.

Well, I am amazed at the minister making that statement.
On January 29, 1942, the minister stated that 10,000 had volunteered for the active army during the month of January, 500 of whom had volunteered the previous day. It is obvious that this great increase in enlistments, gratifying as it is, must seriously congest the training centres, trade schools, and other military establishments for the training of troops. Accommodation is at a premium, and the duties of military instructors will no doubt be severely taxed.
The situation, therefore, is that in October we could not raise a small number of reinforcements for two battalions without including a number of untrained men, and in January our training establishments are overcrowded because of the glut of enlistments. Surely this house must realize that to have called men up on a scientific basis, as they

The Address-Mr. Adamson
were needed, would have been the most efficient way to handle the military man-power required.
In this connection, I quote the experience of the United States armed forces where General Lewis B. Hershey called on Secretary Henry L. Stimson and Secretary Frank Knox to wind up all recruiting of volunteers for the army, navy and marine corps and rely entirely on selective service. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will quote the dispatch:
"America faces the disruption and dislocation of its supply of essential man-power," General Hershey contended.
The army suspended recruiting in December but resumed subsequently after congress had lowered the limit for selective service to 20 years rather than 18 as favoured by the war department.
In his letter he said the appeal for volunteers had lured skilled men from vital production jobs.
General Hershey asserted also that recruiting services were building up a belief that volunteers would be favoured in the military service and commented "such practices are not conducive to good morals."
"An appropriate agency of government should decide where the individual could best serve his nation in total war, rather than leave the decision to the individual who is not a free agent in the matter of such choice," General Hershey contended. He proposed that the recruiting of volunteers be brought to an end gradually to avoid difficulties.
A complete parallel of the position we find ourselves in is to be found in New Zealand where in 1938 the Labour party was elected to power, one of its pledges being "no conscription." In 1940, after the fall of Dunkirk, public opinion became so alarmed that the government of our sister dominion very wisely altered its stand on this question and brought in the national service emergency regulations. These were passed on the 18th of June, 1940, and made public on the 24th of June, 1940. All voluntary enlistments ceased on the 22nd of July, 1940, except in the Royal New Zealand Navy and Royal New Zealand Air Force. The ballot system was introduced for all men between the ages of twenty-one and forty-five, and the bill enacting this measure passed the New Zealand house without a seriously dissenting voice.
As an example of what a small country, whose population is but 1,636,000, can do, I should like to quote the following figures for the record, taken from the New Zealand War Record, an official publication of the government printing office, Wellington, New Zealand: After two years of war, that is in December, 1941. New Zealand had 80,000 men on active service, overseas or in training, 138,000 for home defence enlisted on conditions somewhat similar to our reserve army-

enlisted in civil defence units, making a total of 313,000. Besides this, she had 33,000 applications for enlistment in the air force, of whom 13,500 are, or were at the end of two years of war, actually serving in the Royal New Zealand Air Force. Her operational and air crews overseas were 4,300, as well as 6,000 men volunteered for the navy-4,000 of whom were serving in the New Zealand navy in September as 'svell as 1,000 more New Zealanders in the Royal Navy. To recapitulate:
80,000	active service army overseas or in training; 138,000 home defence units-reserve army; 13,500 air force; 5,000 navy. Total military personnel, 236,500 at the end of September. To this must be added 95,000 in civil defence units, bringing the total for this gallant country, whose population is but one-eighth of ours, to the magnificent figure of 331,000. This was of the date of September, 1941.
New Zealand is, however, not an industrial nation, there being but 11,000 persons engaged directly in munitions manufacture. Therefore it would be unfair to say that on the basis of comparative population Canada's contribution should be 2,650,000 men. It is just this sort of argument and petty mental arithmetic that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) uses when he takes the Canadian enlistments and multiplies by ten to show what the United States army should be compared with ours. You cannot apply the multiplication table to the raising of armies. That is not the way in which an army is raised, and it is this sort of dangerous oversimplification that causes so much ill-feeling and misunderstanding. The way to consider Canada's war effort is to see to it that every man will be called upon to do the job he is most capable of doing. Surely there is no disagreement with that statement.
The unfairness of the present system is that men now doing one job and doing it well can and do alter their calling or occupation almost at will, frequently to the great disruption of industry. I will give one example. In the manufacture of Bren guns there is a very highly technical and skilled job of straightening out

The Address-Mr. Adamson

the barrel prior to its assembly. This is done by hand and by eye, the barrel receiving a series of bumps until it is perfectly true. The trueness of the barrel is judged by the eye of the operator, who observes a series of concentric rings or shadows formed in the barrel, which is highly polished. A great deal of the final accuracy of this magnificent weapon depends upon this operation.
The operators are all young men with peculiarly gifted eyesight. When they engage in this work they are trained for a period of four or five months, and they agree not to go to the movies, not to read, not to smoke, to drink very little, and to do practically no work by artificial light. I am sure the house will agree that these men are working at considerable sacrifice, no matter what they are paid, and that if they change their occupation, it is harmful to the Canadian war effort. Surety it cannot be good to have these very highly' trained men who are doing this excellent work change their position and enter the armed forces unless they can be replaced. Several of these men have enlisted in the Canadian armed forces, against the wishes of their employers, their reasons being those of any red-blooded young Canadian. I suggest that to use these men in the army is not in the best interests of the country's war effort at the present time.
I come now to the present application of the National Resources Mobilization Act. My objection to the present policy of the government is that under the present regulations y'ou have two types of soldiers. This is undignified and entirely foreign to the nature of the Canadian people, and in my opinion Canada believes that the soldier should be a soldier to go where he is sent, to do what he is told to do, to fight the enemy wherever the enemy may be found. To have an. active army battalion in which there are men whose service ends with the three-mile limit is the evil outcome of the mind of a political contortionist, and I warn this government that to continue this policy may have the most serious consequences not only on the morale but on the internal discipline of the unit so affected. A regiment of volunteers which finds itself with an admixture of home defence recruits immediately thinks its fighting day's are over. Morale decreases and resentment against these unfortunate young men grows rapidly.
A regiment is a sacred thing, full of long traditions of great service, full of esprit de corps; and to destroy this fighting spirit is criminal folly which must rest squarely on the shoulders of the government. To have some members of the unit proudly wearing

"Canada" on their shoulders and their regimental badges, while other members do not W'ear these proud emblems, is a disgrace to our military history. It is not only a disgrace to our military history, but is a slap in the face to men of a previous generation whose bravery and endurance contributed so much to our safety here to-day.
The Prime Minister spoke long and loud about the need of preserving national unity. What has he been doing in the past eighteen months? In this very matter of dividing the armed forces into active and home defence bodies he has sown within Canada seeds of disunity and discord which will bedevil posterity with the fomenting of hatred long after he and the rest of the government have passed from the scene.
The great Grecian patriot Pericles, in his immortal speech, bequeathed to the world the conviction that freedom was the right only of those who had the courage to defend it. Those deserve to be free. Yet under our present system it is also given to the faint-hearted and to those who live sheltered lives; they expect the courageous to provide freedom for them.
I have a word to say on the question of a war council of the united powers. It is essential for the prosecution of this worldwide war to act in conformity and jointly with our allies. We have in Washington to-day a United Nations war council for defence on the Pacific; we have in London an imperial war cabinet. Is it for the Prime Minister to say we are not interested in joining both of these bodies? Certainly our highest possible and most accredited military and governmental representatives should be sent to these councils. Not to do so is to accept colonial status. Admittedly we have a joint defence board with the United States, but that is not enough. What goes on in the south Pacific, the fortunes of Singapore, the battle of Libya and the magnificent defence of their country by the soviets are of immediate concern to us. We must be prepared; in fact we must demand, that we be informed of what is being done, and say what we can do and what we are prepared to do about it. If war can be kept at these safe distances, we shall indeed be fortunate. But we cannot expect other nations to be interested in us should we be invaded, unless we are interested in them.
The whole tragic history of the defeat of allied arms in this war has been caused by this narrow nationalism and this inability of nations to act together as a unit. For any responsible Canadian not to jump at the chance, nay, demand that we be included in all of the councils of the United Nations is

The Address-Mr. Adamson
an exhibition of that parochial spirit and an example of the petty political mind that destroyed France.
If, however, we demand this, as I believe we should, we must be prepared to do our part equally and without the slightest hesitation or reserve along with the other United Nations. The government must get out of its mind that Canada is merely contributing something towards the waging of someone else's war. This manifestation of an inferiority complex puts us in a false light. The fact that many of our allies are numerically stronger than we are does not necessarily mean that we have to accept an inferior position all along the line. We must have a say, and an important say, in how the war is to be conducted. And we must be prepared, [DOT] as I have already said, to perform whatever tasks are assigned to us.
There are some who consider that Canada's war effort in this titanic struggle must be of a minor nature. I do not agree with that view. We have a country of twelve million people, a quarter of the population of Great Britain. We have a skilled manufacturing and agricultural manhood. We have natural resources in great abundance. The Prime Minister is prone to talk of Canada as a nation, but every time we are expected to behave as one we immediately revert to the status of a colony. It is essential that we take our active part in both AVashington and London and that we do it without delay. But we must remove the one barrier to ourselves as a nation before we can sit in these conferences of great men, and that one barrier is the lack of an all-out war effort, which includes selective compulsory national service.
Now I come to one more question. I see by the press that there is a movement on foot to take away the wet canteens from the soldiers and to restrict the sale of beer throughout Canada.	Let me warn this
government that if it wants to create bad feeling and to strike a deadly blow at the morale of the Canadian army, the first and surest step to take is to restrict the privileges of the wet canteen. I will ask my friends who are so anxious to interfere with the lives of others to remember that the gallant garrison at Tobruk when they were relieved stated that one of the reasons why their morale remained so magnificently high was the fact that a wise United Kingdom government had seen to it that they had a constant supply of beer.
The discipline of Canadian troops in the city of Toronto during this war has been exemplary. To close the beer parlours or to restrict the sale of beer to his majesty's forces
would shortly bring about the deplorable conditions of the prohibition era and lead to the eventual break-down of respect for law. To do this would be criminal folly.
I have just one word to say to those good people who will accuse me in making that statement. I state that I do not drink beer, nor do I smoke; I do not own any stock in any brewery; I do not know any brewer, and there are no breweries in the riding I have the honour to represent. I merely wanted to make that statement for the record, so that it may be seen that what I have said was said in the interest of the forces and not because I am interested in any other way.
There is one final point that I wish to raise about the speech from the throne, namely, that it contained no mention of Russia. To-day our soviet allies are providing the one bright spot in the picture of world-wide catastrophe. The Russians have been the first people to meet and defeat the blitzkrieg. It is to them we must look for the initial destruction of the German land forces. Their magnificent heroism has sent the brazen horde reeling in disorder from their capital. To-day the soviet power is the second or third most important in the world. Soviet Russia and Canada are near neighbours; we are both northern people living in an extreme climate; we both have a great country to develop. Yet one would think it was almost indecent to mention Russia. I suggest that we should immediately take steps to recognize the government of the Soviet Union. I am glad we had' the statement concerning that of the Prime Minister yesterday. AA^e should welcome in this country a soviet military mission, and should send one of ours to Russia. I believe we have much to teach them, and it is more than likely that they have much to teach us.
I am not afraid of the spread of communism in Canada, if we treat Russia as a full ally and welcome members of her armed forces in the same way as we do those of any of the other "united nations." I should like to see a soviet legation at Ottawa; the hammer and sickle should fly proudly at the masthead instead of being considered an emblem of somewhat questionable morality. I realize that in saying this I may be accused of being a communist or of having communist leanings. I am no communist and no socialist. Some of my friends and all my enemies consider me a reactionary Tory. But to refuse to recognize this great power is building up trouble for ourselves and is going to give great aid to subversive elements which are even now at work trying to undermine the security of the state. We are going to have to admit that the soviet philosophy exists and that it has done
The Address-Mr. Adamson

great things; let us admit it openly and above the broad tables of government rather than have snivelling, subversive agents peddling anarchist literature to the adolescent minds of the students in our schools, universities and training camps We have seen what anarchy has done in other countries. It can happen here.
Listening to the desk-thumping at the close of the Prime Minister's apologia on this plebiscite question, I thought of the words of the poem, "The Fall of the City", by Archibald McLeish:
The city of Masterless men Will take a Master.
There will he shouting then.
Blood after.
Country without leadership; government without direction; parliament without authority.
Canada without leadership.
Shouting now.
Blood after.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on a subject of vital importance. First, however, I should like to say that 'the views I am about to express are my own, and are the result of deep personal convictions. I am quite aware that these views are not shared by many hon. members on this side of the house, but this matter is of such grave importance that it far outweighs any party considerations. In what I am about to say I am considering first of all the interests of the whole country, certainly not those of any political party.
I believe the time is now ripe to wage total war with total war effort. Does anyone here suggest that we have total war effort? How is it possible to have total war effort without the mobilization of all our man-power, wealth and material resources, under a plan of universal compulsory selective service?
As member for the constituency of Eglinton in Toronto, I have received thousands of communications from my constituents, both Liberal and Conservative, with regard to the vital question of selective compulsory service of man-power, wealth and material resources. I greatly welcome the interest taken by my constituents, and at this time publicly thank them for communicating their views to me. I should like to say, however, that prior to receiving this widespread expression of opinion, I had already taken the opportunity of giving to the press my views as a member of par-liment on this vital question. I stated then, as I do now, that I believe the only fair, honest and efficient way to wage total war is by the allocation of our man-power, wealth and

material resources, that is, by introducing a measure of universal selective compulsory service.
I have not arrived at this conclusion hastily and without consideration for the views of others. On this matter, however, which concerns the life and security of every one of us, I felt the time had arrived for me to add my views to those expressed in this house and elsewhere.
I should like to say something about Canada's war effort up to the present. In many spheres it has been a most creditable and substantial contribution. When we consider the difficult task of changing a nation from a peace-time economy to an active wartime economy, I think it becomes us all to pay tribute to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the members of his government for the good work that has been done. In fact I believe it is the utmost pity that in this one most important sphere, the issue of manpower, we should allow the splendid efforts of the government to be overshadowed by the resultant depreciation in civilian morale throughout the land. I realize that this is a job beyond the strength of any one man or group of men to carry on without the cooperation and unity of all men and women in this country.
If we are to carry our full weight forward to victory, it is of the utmost necessity that the people be given inspired leadership, so that our military and material contributions will be supported by a high state of civilian morale. Nazism is a horrible disease which 'has been allowed to run rampant too long. It must and will be destroyed. But let us use every expediency, everything within our power and knowledge to destroy it as quickly as possible before it destroys too many of us.
I should like to state exactly what universal compulsory selective service means to me. It is the complete mobilization of man-power, wealth and material resources, as has been said so often. In the words of the Prime Minister, total war must be met with total-war effort. To that effort there are four parts which go to make up the whole. No two or three parts are of any use or can make up the whole or total effort without the fourth.
First, proper allocation of all Canadians, manhood and womanhood, and proper use of all material resources will do this. [DOT]
Second, men and women who are on the farms, or have knowledge of farming must be kept on the farms. This department of a total war effort I believe to be in a critical stage right now. Farm lands must be kept up to strength, for the food question is equally and as vitally important as the other three parts which make up the whole of total effort.

The Address-Mr. Hoblitzell
Third, our industrial plants and munition factories must not lose their specially trained and skilled labour. Where women can do the work as well as men, they should be conscripted for this work, leaving thousands of men free for the armed services; and all men of the proper age, and fitted to serve in the armed forces, must be trained and equipped to serve anywhere and at any time.
Fourth, all material resources must be wisely appropriated and properly used for the functioning of our war effort.
In my opinion, the voluntary recruiting system has not been a success, particularly in connection with the army. This is not my opinion only; we have the expressed view of our own high military authorities, including Brigadier General Panet and Major-General Vanier, and of course the figures given to this house by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) at the end of the last session, which in themselves were a complete admission that the voluntary system of enlistment was not doing the job. The figures to which I refer were those which he gave the house as to the results of the campaign for 35,000 recruits, which fell short of its objective by approximately 10,000. This speaks for itself.
I despise the backdoor methods, which are a disgrace to our country, of gaining recruits for our aimed forces. I wish you could tell me, Mr. Speaker, how to answer the boys who are constantly coming into my office. These are loyal, patriotic Canadian citizens, anxious to do their duty and ready to serve equality of service. Some tell me they help in or are even the sole support of their families. Even so, they are ready to enlist and do their duty; but, why should they enlist when so-and-so over there, who has no obligations, who is earning good money and enjoying all the comforts of our country, sits back and waits for good opportunities left open by our volunteer recruits? Nor do I approve the disgraceful methods used by some of our recruiting officers, which constitute a system of coercion. Many of these stalwart youths, being just underage for service, are the constant objects of ridicule, sneers and badgering by these same officers. I believe universal compulsory service would be received happily and with deep satisfaction by all the young men of our country. Equality of sacrifice and of service, which far transcends any economic policy, is the only method by which we can defend the system under which we live.
It is true that in the beginning of 1940 our Prime Minister and others gave a pledge to the people of Canada not to instigate conscription for our armed forces for other than home defence, without consulting the people.
But was any government or any prophet in the world at that time able to foresee the sorry and horrible mess into which all the freedom-loving peoples of the world would be thrown by the end of 1941? As I said before, nazism is a disease, and we must keep healthy the place where it is not lest that part also be destroyed. We must go and fight it where where it is.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is my considered judgment that the majority of the people of this country desire that the Prime Minister keep the pledge which goes with his high office, that is, to take whatever measures he and his government feel are wise and necessary to protect the lives and property of the people in the light of whatever perils face the nation. I implore him not to besmirch the honour and dignity of this great dominion by substituting the uninformed opinion of the people for vigorous, courageous and honest leadership. We have seen evidence of the disunity that the proposed , plebiscite is going to create among our people. I therefore plead, Mr. Speaker, through you to the Prime Minister, that it is the course of wisdom for him to arrest this ever-growing dissension of which we all have ample evidence. The simple way would be to provide legislation that will bring into force universal compulsory selective service, both for manpower and material wealth. In this way everyone, regardless of race, colour or religion, who shares the privileges of this country, will equally be called upon to share the responsibilities that go with those privileges.
